Tiny Grimes
JOHP

Interview with Tiny Grimes, JOHP 1
conducted by Bob Kenselaar, November, 1983.
Tape I Side A
Where + when were you born?

Well really the question should be why was I born.
I was born in Newport News, Virginia I think, approximately 7-7-16.
I was always musically inclined, no one
in my family was -- except my mother sang in church --
While I was in school they had
a little band there, and I took
up drums. Well, I was in the
Boy Scouts so that had quite
a bit to do with it. I used to
like drums. So somehow I managed
to get a hold of a set of drums,
And we had a little band called
the oriental serenaders, Huntington
High school. No music was involved --
I didn't know nothing about no
music. We had a swinging little
band, 5 piece band. Joe Jordan
was in there.
How old were you?

I don't know, I no idea.
Somehow, birth certificate got
misplaced, and certain things I
just can't come up with by not
having a family or whatnot.

I played drums and we had
this little band + we used to
play at a little place called Buckrow
Ranch, I think it was, Virginia.
It was a few miles outside of
the town, right on the waterfront,
They had a little dancehall there
and we played there quite often
And then one night there was a flood, and the next night there was no drums, no club, no nothin'. So that ended the drum career right there.
So, I still kept my ears glued to the radio, listening to Duke Ellington, Earl 'Father' Hines. Those two people were idols, musically, you know musically -- that was all you could hear.

I had made up my mind I was going to be a musician, but how? -- because I didn't have no musical learning. I didn't learn in school, they didn't have nothing to play. So I started foolin' around with the piano. I only could play in all the black keys. But that was all right, we got by. We had a little trio called Wynken, Blynken and Nod.

blocks.s: Q. What about in high school?
blocks.x: I left school in the 7th grade. I couldn't afford to go to a school no more. Hit the streets. I was always sellin' papers, shinin' shoes from as long as I can remember.

I tell everybody I wasn't No'd, if you know what I mean. We left Newport News on a truck with about I'd say three or 4 dollars between the 3 of us. Just had enough heart & guts to go out & go to Washington. At that time you could get a meal for about 15¢. We

One fellow was pretty good. He used to imitate Cab Calloway. He did it so good we used to call him Cab. He did his dance & we sang & I played the piano and we entertained over in Washington at the airport was it Alexandria? Anyhow we didn't get but a dollar a night apiece salary and a sandwich & we had to pay the guy to take us over there & take us back. But we stuck with it. Had nothin else to do anyhow. Used to live cheap. Get sick, you just got sick. I used to have tooth aches -- no pain killer, no nothin'.
So we finally left there & went to Washington, approximately '37 or '38, and we did all the amateur shows that was to be did. That's all we could do.
They used to call me Teeny, cause I was so small, but when we got to Washington I changed it myself to Tiny. Sounded a better pronunciation

We hung around Washington for the longest with this Wynken Blynken and Nod Thing gettin' nowhere. So we finally got to New York on a Major Bowes Show. That's quite a few years back -- Major Bowles. He had quite a few people that he hired professionally that you knew were not amateurs, you might say. He would spot them to kind of brighten up the show. So we were one of the groups. We traveled, you know, gettin' nothin' hardly, no money, just to have somethin' to do. We used to go & travel 3 or 4 towns. I was still playing piano.

So finally around 1939 or 40, I got a job with Dickie Wells's -- after hours spot didn't start until about 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning, after everything else was closed. So we had quite a bit of downtown trade, plenty. They used to come up and spend all kind of money. And it was with a tramp band, of all things, 8-piece tramp band. No horns, kazooks.

Bill Pemberton played bass, of all people... We had a hell of an 8-piece band. 3 guys Kazooks, sing and you would think it was a whole band up there. And this was in around 1940, the first part of 1940. As of so.
As far as the guitar it was a lucky incident that I learned it. Cause hanging out with fellas that had a group when they had guitars-- tipple. You know what a tipple is?--Ten string guitar.

My hand wasn't quite big enough to fit the whole guitar. So I used to fool around with the first four strings. I found myself progressing. No one to learn from or nothing, no lessons and all that stuff, just goin'.

So I locked myself up in a room for about weeks and weeks, just me + the guitar trying to get it together cause I couldn't read I'd have sheet music and I'd try to get the diagrams off there but they would mess me up because they were for ukulele. They weren't guitar chords, and I couldn't get the hang of that so, I just kept after it-- goin' to clubs, the after hours spots, Monroe's after hours spot. Didn't cost nothin' to get in, just go and listen

I started learning the guitar, but I was still playing the piano. I'd lay the guitar on top of the piano. But first of all the way I got a guitar was out of a pawn shop for 5 dollars. I just had to have one but I couldn't afford nothin'. But what the guy had -- four strings -- was what I wanted anyhow, so that's how the four strings happened -- I never did graduate. In fact I tell everybody I could never afford the other two strings.

I just kept after it... After I found out I could do a little somethin' with the four I didn't see why I needed the other two in the first place (I did what I wanted to do as far as the four strings. I just left it that way. And a fella named Eddie Bell gave me credit, & that's how my first electric guitar came in. It wasn't a guitar, it was an electric banjo. Great long neck, but I tuned it D like the first 4 strings of a guitar. I played it. I used to get gigs in about 3, to 4 months. I was playin' good enough to get little gigs. And in 7 months I was with Cats & the Fiddle. I had only been playing 7 months.
Piano.
I could only play in the black keys & it was all by ear. I never took a lesson in my life. I just could hear what was right & what was wrong. And that's the only

that kept me with Art Tatum. There was no music involved. I just could hear. A lot of people think that playing 4 strings is easy to play but its not. You've got to a lot of jumpin' about -- miss notes. Better run to cover when you run out of strings, As far as range...

Now the piano -- I first learned it. I don't know how I learned. I just kept foolin' around with it to accompany ourselves 'cause we did a lot of singing. So I came out, I'd say 75 to 90 % right compared to music, which I didn't know anything about, Just listenin' and playin'.
Did you sing?

That's that I was one of the main voices. That's why they took me in the Cats and the Fiddle, because I was replacing a fella, the guy you hear, the high tenor... I was one of the few cats that could play and sing at the same time. If you notice a lot of guitar players if they're singing they don't play. If they're playin' they ain't singin'... To play them together, the coordination is very awkward, hard to do. But I could do that sing the words & make my chords & everything else.
As a kid.
We did Fats Waller tunes -- Honey suckle Rose. Everyday songs. I remember that
one distinctly. Cab Calloway tunes. Nothing We just did the everyday songs, extraordinary. Trio songs, like the Andrews Sisters.

Q. Dancing
I was a tap dancer. I was very much in earnest. I tried everything to be in show business. They had a place called the Hoofers Club, the Rhythm club. And all the fellas used to meet down there, when they had nowhere else to go. Nothin' but dancers.

Round 132nd & 2nd Avenue, somewhere near there. I'd go down there to play the piano. That's why I was in the show downtown, the off-Broadway show, Cause I know how to play for dancers. Then I wind up learnin' how to dance myself. Cause I liked it. I could keep up with them pretty good. ... This must have been '38 or '39, yeah. Somewhere like that, dancein'.
But I was still playing piano -- playing at the piano. But I could understand, I could play for dancers good, and they liked the way I played.

... When I got with Art Tatum out in California I had only been playing about a year and a half -- year, and seven months, somewhere like that. But you see those fellas when we got to California with Cite and the fiddle we got a few weeks work & then we didn't get any. And then we got a job to come back to the Apollo -- we had played there several times. All the way back from California to NY and pay your own fare, for a hundred and some dollars. The fare cost more than for me gettin back here. I just say, well look, I just stay out here. And that's when I met Tatum. We started playin', I got a few jobs, joined the union out there. And then Slim of Slim & Slam got put in the army. And Slim asked me to take his place, which was impossible. Nobody could take Slim Gaillard's place. But I was the only available guitarist there so you know we worked together and I did the best I could. ...

... We used to go to this place called Lovejoys and sit around and jam. We did it every night and the first thing you know there was a crowd. And then Tatum used to come down & play and we had the place jumpin'. The guy would give us a sandwich and maybe a drink. And we come to find out, even now and then we'd look, we see a chain at the door & a crowd of people outside. Now he's gettin' a turnover makin' a handful of money and we ain't gettin' a dime.

And we didn't even realize it. He'd let a group of people out, the place would fill up + we played. No brains. Play and play and play. Till some guy spotted us. in [from?] The Streets of Paris, out on Hollywood and Vine and induced him to put a trio together. And It was a hit right off the reel.
I wasn't the entertainer that Slim Gaillard was --

Slim and I, when we got through playing, thats where we'd end up. Everybody else would be there. They called it Big Leg Chicken. And we would all just gather. It was a gatherin' place. So we started bringin' our instruments down just playin' to have something to do. That's when Fats came in. All I know is he was playin' and somehow or another he didn't mind us joinin' in, or somethin' like that. And the trio formed right from there, thats all I can remember.
* I don't even know who brought him there or how we met, I can't even remember that part.
No formal introduction, and all that stuff. "Is it all right we sit in and play, man" "yeah" That was that.
playing with Tatum.

It was an honor but it was no pleasure He made it hard. It was hard. There was never a rehearsal, not show you somethin'. or [he would] say, "no that don't go like that that go like this" or "what's the name of that chord" Whatever I learned I learned it on the bandstand. Everything, sittin' on the bandstand playing. We never had a rehearsal. And when he started playing, man, you just had to do the best you could to try to keep up. It was somethin' else. It was a hell of an experience.
Did Tatum select all the material?

We both would set riffs, and if the riff fitted and he liked it it stayed there. He wasn't a demanding guy, "You gotta do it this way, you gotta do it that way" Automatically we thought alike, if it fitted it stayed there. If he didn't play it no more then you knew it didn't belong there. So you just left it alone. That's the way that went. But if he joined in and played it with you, then that's cool.
Comet sides pretty heavily arranged.
They were all made up on the bandstand & we used to try to outdo each other playing little ditties from different songs and stickin'
em in and make sure that they fit.
Who started that?

I did, and I overdid it. Because a guy wrote me up about it and said 'he's all right, but he plays too many of those things'. But all of us was doin' it. Not only me, but I guess I did it a little more than the rest. But it was a challenge among ourselves. Then when everybody else started doin' in Ella do it all the time, Sarah Vaughan all then. Nobody said nothin' about it. And they still do it. But like I said, I probably overdid it.
Cat and the Fiddle.

You had to have a pretty strong brain to remember. Everything was remembered. There was no reading. They had all this singing, all the parts, we would rehearse, and I had to learn about 20 or 30 songs when I first joined them in order to get by. So we would rehearse about a week and I got enough songs for us to get going and bit by bit after awhile I knew everything they knew. Plus I did a lot of the arranging. They got a little bit more on the musical side, I'd say. Like I arranged Blue Skies...
Electric guitar

Eddie Bell ... finally found me a guitar, a four string guitar, I don't know where he got it from but it was electric. I think he made it, I'm not sure. I know it was no more. It was a Gibson. ... they owned a store on 48th St, and Broadway...
What made you want to play electric guitar?
So I could be heard. Especially after I started hear Charlie Christian. But you couldn't hear nothin worthwhile. that sound, that new sound, the amplifier really changed things around.
Snag
Who else influenced you on guitar
446 ... Snags Allen ... Skeeter Best ... Jerome Dahl, who plays with Jonah Jones ... I learned the hard way.

466 Snags Allen, they had a heck of a group called the Harlem Highlanders. And you never seen nothin like that. I tried to revive it a few years later. If they had the right manager, the boy it was a million dollar act. All dressed in kilts. And they could dance, sing, I played piano for them at times. A fella named Bobby Lawrence
one of the greatest dancers in the world---
Type I, Side B
I loved to go fishin'. I used to make a little light living crabb'in and cookin' crabs, sellin' papers, shinin' shoes, I did everything....

...I'm quite sure they could have gotten somebody else, there's no gettin' around that... But I think I got an A for effort 'cause I tried. We used to be workin' at a place anywhere and during the intermission they would be looking for me, and I'd be downstairs in the dressing room struggling with the guitar. That's where they had to come get me. That's how bad I wanted to try to keep up. I called myself the low man on the Tatum pole. I tried. I was trying... But some smart all sky agent convinced him he could make as much money by himself as he could with the trio, but it didn't work. A shame, it didn't work. So by that time I was somewhere else, I don't know where the hell I was. Cleveland, I stayed there two years. [Tatum] got Everett Barksdale on guitar, they lasted a while....
Los Angeles

Streets of Paris... we stayed out there the longest time. Then somehow or other we got a call to go to New York. We went to this place called the 3 Deuces. And we stayed there a long, long time. And then we went out, Cleveland, Chicago, we went everywhere. We were in demand. Didn't have the right agent.
Who was the agent
--- Aguy associated with William Morris, he was the cause of everything breaking up ---
... We'd like to have gotten in a good picture, but Nat Cole beat us out. I played the music for Moke and Poke in "Stormy Weather." I used to rehearse them, the two dancers.
California was hip we used to have a ball out there. We didn't want to leave --- the only place to jam was where we were at.
Who came to the jam sessions?
Everybody, King Cole. Everybody that was out there at that time. ---
... Vincent Minelli, Jack Benny ---
Did Lester Young
Did you play with Lester Young out there?

Sure, I used to go to his house every day. Lester had a thousand records I guess. And he sit up there and play all day every day. He loved his play, he loved his horn. I used to go out to his house. --- He lived on the other side of town --- I had a little old Ford. --- He and what's the bass players name, Charles? Best bass player in New York. Fight all the time. --- We used to get together and jam.
... Everybody loved T-Bone. ... He was King of the blues ...
The other fella I was trying to think of ... was Charles Mingus. ...
And Irving Ashby ... was the guitar player, with Hamp. And we used to get together and have sessions. I still was green as grass, I didn't have no idea -- a note to me looked like a piece of Greek.
And another fella, excellent guitar player, John Collins. ...
... Bumps Meyers ...
...only tenor play I knew was Big -- somethin' Big George? ---
Q. New York Jam Sessions

... I was just learning how to play -- I used to go down to Clark-Monroe's, told, Wilson used to be there. All the great guys used to come there. I had in my mind to play ... they asked me --- whisper it in my ear, say "hey man, look I'm gonna play somethin' here so you lay out, hear?" That musta been how bad I was. But I was determined. I couldn't keep up with some of them cats. But I finally found myself doin' enough to keep up with them, and get a little gig every week end hopefully 5 dollars, 3 dollars, and There were some good times. I wasn't no dog-eat-dog like it is now. You could walk over to central park and sit out there and sleep out there all night, and nobody would bother you. Walk the streets at night.
Did you ever play with Charlie Christian

Didn't I tell you he played my guitar? -- At Morton's, everybody used to meet at Morton's -- Monk, Joe Guy, Kenny Clarke, his brother -- a lot of people don't know his brother played bass. Charlie Christian was there all the time. I'm just learnin' how to play. So I come in and Charlie has taken my guitar

And played it, played the hell out of it, 4 strings -- he played it. And that made me wanna play that much worse, ha, ha. He was a nice cat. He was tickled at me for the 4 strings. He said, "man why don't you get yourself six strings". I say, "I can hardly play these four, no sense of six." He played it all right, old Gibson I had. But he could play, I got some tapes around here. Dan Morgenstern has got the tapes. He's got the records --
Q. Cats and the Fiddle record dates, Songs composed by TG

Those guys had a thing of doing that I didn't know anything about. See, they were together, they started off together before I joined them. They would put everything wrote by the Cats and the Fiddle. Me, I don't know what did I know. If I was smart, if I had somebody to tell me ... but I made them all get a share, but I still never got a share. Red Buttons say, "Ain't never got a dinner." I never got a share. I wrote a lot of stuff. And I arranged all that those that was arranged. No music, just with a head, I had to come from the head.
Q. Record dates.

The record dates, they were all right. Cause we know what we were doing. Wasn't nobody nervous or no nothin' cause we were workin together all that time. No problem, you know. We didn't have a drum. And I wonder now how they kept such good tempo, good time 'cause we didn't have no drum. I guess that's why I'm so tough on drummers. They don't play the drums all the way. A lot of them play like they sprained their ankle, know what I mean? ~~Bass drum~~ like the bass drum-- foot hurt or somethin'. Now and then they'll get the bass, but I mean you have to be like Jo Jones he's a drummer, man. His bass and his foot and everything, they goin' at the same time. And a few more of them. But for an example you know. A lot of guys get a foot peddle there and hardly never use it. . . .
Tunes with Cats & the fiddle.
~~We~~ We worked, and we rehearsed, you had to rehearse to remember all that stuff. Everybody had to do his part.
Had you written songs before this, for other bands?

Yeah. I like to have two good chances but somehow or other fate let them go. Louis Armstrong was gonna do Swingin In the Groove. And it fitted him perfectly. So was Louis Jordan But my song came up last and by that time
They were tired, they said, "well, we do it next time.
How did you get the song to Louis?

I don't know I think I bugged everybody, ha ha. I just bugged everybody. Didn't nobody write -- I don't think it was wrote out. I believe I hummed it. We had the words wrote. But there was no music, 'cause I don't remember nobody writing no music. But by the time he got to it he had been goin' for about 3 or 4 hours. By hummin' it to him, trying to get him. He liked it all right. But just didn't have the time.
Had you written those tunes for this group? (C+F)

I just wrote 'em just so. For this particular group I had wrote a couple of theme songs one to go on & one to come off. Introduction, you know. We sang and called every body's name & we went off. I still use it when we go off now. George Kells uses it quite a bit.
What song is that?

We hope you like our music, we did the best we could And if you heard your favorite song we hope that it was good We're going but we'll be back so everybody have a drink You have one & I'll have one, it's later than you think.
It's got music to it.

And I have a fish song that it ever got to Sesame Street or somewhere like that it would go over. It's called 'I don't care how fast a fish may swim that he'll never sweat.' I recorded it in Paris, but it didn't mean anything over there. I never recorded it here but I do it a lot. I did it on a Jack Kleinsinger concert and we had 700 people sing it -- audience participation. 700 people sang 'He'll never sweat.' It goes over good...
Cats & the Fiddle -- had they been looking for an electric guitar player

That part I don't know. But the thing of it is they offered it to Snags, the same guy I was talkin' about. And somehow or other he didn't want to leave town or he had something, I forgot. Anyhow, he referred me. And I really gave 'em an audition, in a way of speaking. They say we gonna get together & we hear you play, and they heard me play & the band say 'yeah.' -- By the way, they didn't know if I could sing or not...
So they were happy and they talk to me, but man the money I got was -- mmmh! Nothin'. But anyhow I was happy to get off

the ground ... big time group -- first thing we hit was the Apollo Theater. I couldn't believe I was on the stage -- sittin' up there lookin' out. But they went over, they went over very good, 'cause they had this hit song, I Miss You So.
Was that one of the first jobs you played with them, at the Apollo Theater?

When we started off -- No, I think we went to Chicago or somewhere. They had to break me in good first, you know. But the first job I think we went to Chicago, 'cause he had a couple of cars [?]. We returned to the Apollo Theater -- it was packed, cause it was between the Ink Spots and ourselves, running neck and neck. The Ink Spots were ahead, not neck and neck. They were ahead, but we were right on their heels. They took off, boy.
2nd record date w/ C & F. George Steinbeck replaced Chuck Barksdale on bass, ...
Oh yeah, George, yeah. Very good bass player. Think Chuck got sick, I believe. Went back to Chicago. Anyhow George, he was a good solid bass player -- he was with Basil for a while I think.
Tunes you did at that session --
I arranged Blue Skies; Stomp, Stomp I made up --
Get along well with other guys in C & F.

Yeah, sure, we got along good. Had to 'cause we had to rehearse daily. It was no let up. Because they had such a repertoire and I had to learn all these things and the parts that go with 'em, not just sing in the lead -- harmony. I was enthused. I enthused them. I had new stuff. The piano helped, and everything helped, and we had a little dance goin'.
Did you dance with them too?
Yeah. I was an asset. I was an asset to the group.
Another song you recorded with them was Lawdy Claudy.
Oh yeah. Another thing I made up. I don't know if I played piano on that, I know it was a saying at that time a hot saying, you know, like slang, as you might say, so I made a song out of it.
You left Los Angeles with Tatum for New York with Tatum and played at 52nd street.

Yeah we went to a place called the Three Deuces. I think I mentioned that. Stayed there weeks and weeks. Everyone used to come down there. A great singer used to come down there every night. Bailey, Mildred Bailey used to come down there all the time. I mean everybody came there, no way around that. We even did The March of Dimes or March of Times or somethin there. . . . They show it every now and then now. . . . We were in and out, we left there like I said, we went out west, come back, some place.
March of Time, was that a film short?
It was a film, yeah.
What did you play?
My song, Tiny's Exercise, sure did.
When did you write that tune, was it while you were with Tatum?
I believe so, I think so, yeah. I'm quite sure of it.
Did it start as an exercise?
Well when I would be practicing this riff came out. And I just named it that.

Because it sounds somethin' like an exercise, not that I could read an exercise. That's the way it came out. I just added a few more touches & changed the music. It came out pretty good. Tatum liked it. He played it all the time. Only thing, it was my tune but he played it too fast, ha ha, I could hardly keep up with it. Ike Quebec -- I made it with him also.
What was 52nd Street like?

Just like the Village is now, only more so and more pleasant. There was no lot a bunch of nuts hungin around all the time. It was just pleasant down there. Pleasant place to go and hang out and not get bugged by nobody. Even the bars.
Tape two
--- Oscar Moore, excellent guitar player --- Floyd Smith was an excellent guitar player. He was with Andy Kirk a long time. I got in trouble trying to play his blues. learn how to play his blues ---
When did you first meet Floyd Smith?
--- I went to one of there rehearsals and just listened, you know, Admired his playing. He was colorful. But I never
met him to really know him. Not until long time --- Atlantic City then I knew him fairly good, cause he played up the street.
Did he influence you?
No, he didn't influence me.
Remember making records in LA w/Tatum?
No, we didn't make any records dates. Well at that time you couldn't make no records anyway. You had to be blackmail, if you made any, and the material wasn't any good -- during the war. ---
... In Cleveland I think we made some glass records, covered with some kind of substance. ---
Did you make records for the armed services?

yes, we called em V-discs. Made quite a few of those V-discs. And also made some for that, what was the name of that corporation trying to get together --- blue and white label --- started with a C ---
We made a lotta --- little bits small records. I think that was when 45's were
just about ready to come out.
Do you remember much about the musician's union recording ban?
No, I don't remember anything about that, nope.
Did you did many radio broadcasts with Tatum?

I remeber one outstanding one with Art Tatum. There was a place in Cleveland we used to broadcast from. A chinese restaurant... They had a broadcast about twice a week... I forget the name of it, but it was a high-class restaurant and we broadcast from there - And that's about the only thing I know as far as broadcast.
Did you do broadcasts on NBC?
-- No, not that I can remember...
What else do you remember about the broadcast with Paul Whiteman.

-- The only thing that stood out in my mind was it was such a big band they had there and then the three of us. To me it was competitive, in a way of speaking... I said 'bt ga, "Look at all these guys -- violins & things & harps," I say "just do the best we can." Well, we were never a nervous group. We wea went to play we just played. I just had a harder time than anyone else. Cause trying to play 4 string
guitar and keep up with him is no picnic.
Did Tatum know that you didn't read music?

Oh yeah. He didn't read music. Nobody read no music. We had no time for no music. I don't know if Slam could read or not, even. Maybe, I really don't know. I know I didn't. Shit, never crossed my mind to read no music. I have faked it quite a few times. I mean faked it too, I faked it in Germany about 5 years ago or 6 years ago --- This one was with Sonny Payne, we were in Frankfurt not Frankfurt -- right next to Frankfurt... Anyhow it was over there with a 70 piece symphony band with Odetta as star. And 5 bass players, harps. Milt Buckner was there... And they laid out all this music, you know. Well see, they were rehearsing, you know what I mean, they had to rehearse, they had to get Odetta's music together. And 70-piece symphony band. And the funny part about it was it was a little embarassing but I say I didn't care. 'Cause when I opened up my guitar and the german people in the band they started snickering saw these 4 strings they started snickering, ha ha. I say, with hell with them. Let them get their parts. Now they got all this great big sheet of music

About 5 of 'em. Now me like I said, looked like Greek to me. Although this was about six years ago, I could read fairly good, but this was out of sight. So I didn't say anything, I just listened. And they rehearsed all day, for the next day, and by the time they were ready to go to work the next day I had mine, just by listening. I knew exactly what to do -- my little interlude and whatnot. (haha) But this couldn't touch Art Tatum or Slam, they couldn't touch 'em. Those guys, you could blow an automobile horn or tinkle a glass & they could tell you exactly what note it is. Perfect pitch, you know. I couldn't do that. I don't know how they did it. But they would get into arguments. Sometime it would be between the keys, that they would know. But it could hear musically if it was wrong -- you keys playin' it and I'll get it. But there comes a time when they ain't got no time -- listenin' -- and then trouble is there. I managed to get by with it.
So, you got along well with Tatum?

Oh good, we had no problems. I used to call him uncle. He used to call me Grimey Joe, Grimey Joe. All the time Grimey or Grimey Joe I said, 'All right uncle'. You're my uncle.' He didn't like me say 'I ain't your uncle.' We had a good time. We had no problems. Never. The whole time I was with that group

I missed -- I was late once. I just overslept. I didn't have a clock. We were in Washington at the Howard Theater and boy when I woke up, I said "oh no" mmhm. I did it, finally did it, and when I got there, they was on the stage. Ain't nobody said a word though. They didn't chastise me, they didn't say a word. I wish they had something -- ha ha, they knew it wasn't no habit of mine, they knew that something was wrong. I just didn't get up. But that was the only time. I'd always be the first one downstairs practising, trying to get my part. Les Paul used to come & listen to us.
Where was that?
In California. Buddy Rich used to come and sit in with us, while he was in the Army. Right in The Streets of Paris.
If I had the knowledge to know that I have then or the know-how... If I had somebody to help me, I'd have been much better.
Did you try to get Tatum to help you out?

Well you see, no. See the only thing was once we finished the job it was straight home. Everybody went their separate ways. A lot of times we used to meet uptown, and sit at an after hours spot. And a lot of times he would be up there he'd be up there playing, you know

just sittin' up playing. And no time to ask nobody like them. Because all the other piano players were around trying to catch him off guard, or that type of thing. That's why you have to practice a lot or they step right on your nose. They're waitin' for you. But like they couldn't touch him... They'd keep 'em off him. I was... more competitive than it is now. Friendly, competitive, you know what I mean. Try to outplay each other. New guy would come into town, you know what I mean... think he smart... go up into a pool room and wash him away.
Did you try to get Slam Stewart to help son out with the arrangements.

No, like I said when we finished playing, everybody went his way... I guess they just figured, you know your instrument, you're a musician. It wasn't a matter of getting together unless you were a band, you know.
Like Cats and the Fiddle?
Yeah, yeah. Well we had to, we had a four voice thing goin' there, we had to. But I mean the three of us we just played, just sat down to play in a hell of a song way.
I Got Rhythm way up in tempo. And we'd talk about baseball or football. You know, like there was nothin happenin. Like we were holdin a conversation. On the bandstand.
Do you remember any outstanding places that you played.

The Paul Whiteman thing was outstanding. The whole thing was outstanding. I had no time to time to enjoy, arrest or to do nothing. Even when I got home, I was just me & the guitar. But if I just had someone to show me to say "no, you could do it this way, or you could do it that way." Or any kind of help. But I just figured it out myself. And I would up when I did learn, I learned the wrong fingering. Unorthodox fingering, you know, not the correct way. That's why now when I play, I don't play with my little finger unless I'm playing chords. And you're supposed to use your little finger, along with everything else. I just learned, I did the best I could with the tools I had. As long that it came out pretty good, that's all that mattered.
Do you remember much about the record date you did for Brunswick in early 1940? You did played I Got Rhythm & Cocktails for two, I Ain't Got Nobody, After you've gone
Moonglow... I would do anything for you, Liza, Tea for Two, Honey, suckle Rose.
We did all that many? I didn't know we did that many. Some of 'em was for, what do you call that -- What's the one that started with a "D", Decca...
Bluebell or something... They had a subsidiary... What were the name of the Cats? The Riddle.
Blue bird.
Wasn't that RCA?
When did you first hear Tatum?

I heard him hear when I was playing piano & just starting on the guitar. And he used to come to a little spot in the basement. And James P. Johnson, Tremble & Chisholm some guy named Chisholm... and they all used to melt up there for a cutting session, they called it. And I used to go up there listening, and I called myself a piano player. But I had never met him, I never said anything to him, or nothin'. I just sat around listening.

And these cats when I got thru playing I'd say "what the hell am I doin' even looking at a piano?" But at that time I had been looking for something else to start with. That's where the guitar came in. So I had heard him first, but I didn't know him. He was with playing with this Adelaide something... Adelaide Hall I think I believe. Whoever it was, that introduced him into New York. And everybody was on his tail. All the piano players was on his case. You know, when they find a new cat come town, that can play, you know they watch for him. And they gathered him all up. But you see what he did, he let 'em all play, he wouldn't touch the piano until everybody played. And there must have been about ten of 'em, and they played, and they played. I mean they played. This cat would come & sit down & wash them all -- made you forget the other ten. ha ha! He made them forget themselves. He was something else, man. I don't know how that cat did it. And have himself a bottle of beer, Pabst Blue Ribbon Beer. Quart of a bottle of beer in one hand and playing with the other & you'd think there were three people up there. That's how I first heard him. Then the next time -- way years later -- that I found myself playing with the same cat I couldn't believe it. Jammin' with him anyhow. That's why I tried so hard. I tried awful hard! ... I gave it my best shot.
Did you rely on sheet music at all?
I had sheet music, but I was looking at the diagrams, it turned out that the diagrams were for ukulele & that didn't work. --- thing was tuned wrong.
How did you tune your guitar?
Like the first four of a six string. EBGD. I never had no more to by those two strings. ---
I'm tired now, man.
When you were jamming with Fats at Lovejoy's, was he playing at Street of Paris at that time.

Yes yes, he was playing there, he had been there quite a while. Playing a solo. There were two rooms, one was downstairs, one was upstairs. He played at the downstairs room 'cause they had a little a pretty nice band called Big Six... he was the tenor player -- very good, they had a hell of an outfit. But they never got nowhere. They stayed there, they were the house band. He was the house pianist. So, when he would get through, he would go to this after-hours spot cause there wasn't any where else to go. Lovejoy's Big Leg Chicken, that was the name of it.
What was a typical night like when you were at the Streets of Paris?

Average, just average. A lot of celebrities used to come in, you know. But it was such a big room. It was awful big even for the band upstairs it was pretty big. large. But the music lovers, when they came, they came to hear Fats -- So much talk -- Although the man is the most underrated person -- among the underrated that ever was ever alive. I mean too much talent, they got too much talent, they hurt their own selves, looks like. That kind of a thing is possible, you know, you can be too good for your own self. To me if Fats just had a little flash, a little jive, a little whatever. But that wasn't him. He was serious. When he sat down to the piano he played -- there was no clowning. But if he had just had just any little gesture, you might say, that wouldn't have hurt his playing, I mean, look at Earl Garner, he growled more growled more than he played -- haha -- you could hear him growling -- Hamp would be hollering -- Slam, you know? A little gimmick you might say is the only thing in my eyesight that held him back, as far -- Not that he wasn't the greatest piano player in the world, but if he just had a little flashes something to do. Look at Ray Charles -- dances on the piano -- I'm not

talking about the singing part - although he could sing the blues. Excellent. A lot of people didn't know that. He could sing the blues very good. I don't know why he didn't add 'em in there in our little program.
How about when you used to quote a lot from popular songs. Was that the kind of thing that helped make Tatum a little more popular at least when you were with him?

Well as far as most people, but a lot of the critics used to pan especially me. Like I said I may have overdid it but that was a challenge among the three of us. See who could think of something that could fit in. We had been doing that for the longest, and a couple of critics didn't like it. . . . We played the songs straight first, before we started doing the little gimmicks and things. . . We played the song as it should be, then we started ad libbin' and in I think it was Flying home we got over 20 thing in there, ditties as you might say. I made up a lot of 'em. It was a challenge among the three of us. . . .
Now they do it in modern times, and they take another song and put another melody to it and it's the same song, but they make it an original.
Streets of Paris, was it a mostly white club?
Yeah it was white, white. Cause it was way out, and Hollywood, the transportation has never been too good... And we was playing way in the heart of town...
Did black people come to streets of Paris at all?
Yeah, they came, but it was not as much as other types of people...
But it wasn't a segregated club?
No no no. Hell, no. They had a black band there. Big six or something. We were black so it was no segregated thing, no.
Was it a nice place?
Yeah...
Did a lot of musicians come...
Yeah...
...First thing I know we were in New York,...
How did you travel to New York?
Train... We had compartments, ... We all came together...
So you got to know 'em pretty well?
Yep, yep, that's a between yep cause I could never hang out with him I mean,
You mentioned the owner of the Street of Paris, do you remember much about him?

...I never got to know him too good... He recognized the music. Some how he heard we were over there playing, especially Fatum his man that was working for him playing over there, he say "What the hell he doin' over there playin' every night for free". And the trio was gotten formed at the time & we didn't know we were just havin' fun. Till finally one night Fatum told us, he said "Look, we're gonna play out here" I don't know what the words were,....
...The other thing we had over there wasn't much when I took Slim's place...
Did you sing with Slam?

A little, 'cause I had been with the GF + I could sing harmonies, but like I wasn't a showman see Slim, I mean how do you follow him. Not me... Not at that particular time. But I wound up being another Redd Foxx and everything else. Tell jokes, dance, sing do everything else.
How did you travel with Tatum?

Train. We didn't do that much traveling. We stayed at places so long. After the 3 Peaces I think we went to Cleveland, and played at a place called Chin's. I think a Chinese place. We even broadcast from there. We stayed there quite a while. But we never got to Toledo, his home, I don't know why. We went to Chicago.
Did you ever get a chance to travel back to your old home town?
Virginia you mean. No, I went back there once, that was enough for me.
You don't have any family there at all?
No...
To digress a bit... Did you know your parents at all?

No I didn't know them that well. She stayed in the Church a lot, and I was out in the street. Shiniw shoes -- I'd be gettin' up 5 o'clock in the mornin' sellin' newspapers -- The Times-Herald. I did the regular hustle that the fellows do. There was no robbin' and stealin' like they do now...
Date of birth sometimes given at 1917, not 1916 as you said before.

Well, to me that's approximately right, although I remember when I was real young and still footin' around with the piano I had a little job at a cleaning & pressing place called Joe Frank's. It was like over town you would call it, -- other side of the bridge and tracks -- when you went over the bridge and tracks you were in the white neighborhood. So somehow or other I got a job working for -- they gave me a little Ford that I wrecked about ten times. A little truck, to deliver clothes. I could keep whatever cleaning that I got, and that was the deal. I didn't get no salary. I learned how to press clothes. I pressed clothes in Washington -- If I had stayed down there I'd have did a lot better much better than I'm doing up here, I'll tell you. 'Cause I would have had a cleaning and pressing joint -- establishment, Because I knew the business, I'd see how they dyed, and all the equipment --
Did you travel by car at all when touring with Tatum?

Not that I can remember. I got a little tiffed off at him 'cause he wouldn't do me a favor one time. I thought I deserved it. He didn't have to do it. One wound up he knew better than me. I just had to have this car. This was in New York (at the Three ---). So this high-pressure salesman sold me a --- one of the first cadillacs with the automatic shift. Anyhow the war was on... It was a good car. And I couldn't get enough money to get the downpayment + he wouldn't give it to me. And I get mad... not mad, you know what I mean... Somehow or other I get it and the first time I took him for a ride the clutch wouldn't work -- we got stuck in Central Park. Oh man, then he got mad. He said "I told you not to buy that thing. But that was the only thing that was wrong with it, the clutch needed adjusting... Anyhow it must have took us about an hour to get through Central Park going along about 3 or 4 miles an hour... You could smell the breaks burning, oh boy, he was sick of me, ha ha. He never rode in no more.
What were the places that you played like?
... We didn't play too many places because when we got to a place they kept us. We ended up in

Washington, at some little club, I don't know what the name of it was... We stayed down there a long time. That was one of the first times that we had decided, because we met at the club every day, it was open, we'd set down there and play -- give a free matinee. We loved playing, just play, if we were somewhere, we played. And they had a piano and we said, we're gonna have a rehearsal. And we tried to have this rehearsal on Minuet in G, but the people in the club, they don't wanna hear no rehearsal. "Play, man," you know, and they get on your nerves. So they got on our case and we had to leave it go and play or go home. So we played a while and then I think we left. That's the only time there was an attempt to rehearse. And we didn't ever get the piece. So that was that.
You said that you didn't read music at this time but did you know how to read chord symbols?

No, I just knew that they sounded right. When I had a sheet of music I would look at these diagrams they had, where they show you how to put your fingers. And some of them had six strings, but most of them were ukulele charts, and I would make this thing and try to go along with the song and it didn't come out right. Because the way I had my fingers and the way the uke is tuned And I'd make sure

I would sit there for 15 minutes with just that one diagram trying to figure out, and ... I know I'm putting my fingers right. And I come to find it was for ukelele. But they didn't have the name. If they had said 'for ukelele' then I wouldn't have bothered with it in the first place.
So Tatum wouldn't ever call out changes to you?

No, he just went ahead and played. And I caught it as it went along. Like it was coming through the air and I would just reach up and grab, you know. Whatever he played, he just played... After Slam was no trouble, I was the one, like I said, I was the low man on the Tatum pole.... Boy, I'd go down stairs I'd be practicing.
Did you ever practice scales?

No, no scales. I wouldn't even know what the scales were, it was the song that I had to learn. And if they were playing and I didn't know, I'd go downstairs by my self and see if I could get it. And I'd get it most of it. Most of the time if we played it a couple of times, I had it, whatever it was. And he never complained so evidently I must have been playing it right.
Did you ever copy things off of records?
No, I didn't have a record machine. I just never had no record machine for a long, --- It came from the radio, everything I learned, radio.
People have said you sounded a lot like Charlie Christian.

He was a big influence. Because the things that he played I had in mind to play a long time. That's the way I wanted -- before I even heard him. It wasn't a matter of copying. It was a matter of -- I'd have to associate it with Ross Columbo and Bing Crosby. They both sounded alike. So it wasn't a matter of somebody copying somebody. --- A lot of people sound alike. Just like a lot of people fares no kin, but they look alike -- look like they come from the same family. So, it wasn't a matter of me copying, I mean the things he played, if you notice, there is not that many of his riffs, it's just the sound, and the style. Not that many of his riffs on none of my records. Some of the things I have played, Soft Winds I played --- Profamelly Blue. But I mean 90% overall you don't find me doing his riffs. You'll hear maybe now and then. But the sound, we sounded alike. I didn't copy him. If I was copying him I could have never did it that quick. --- It just come natural. --- We just happened to think that way. That's the way I look at it.
Radio broadcast for Philco Hall of fame on NBC in 1944 in New York
No...
How about the June 26, 1944 record date for Asch records? ... They later issued excerpts from sort of a rehearsal of it...

Yeah I have it here now. I was surprised that they would do a thing like that, but I mean, collector's item thing, they consider that very valuable. They did it I'm amazed... Now that's a sort of -- I wouldn't call it a rehearsal, it's just tellin' us what to do & how to do it, & that's that. The way he wanted it. I can remember that he was tellin' me to do somethin'. I don't even remember what song it was. We were gettin' something together. It was probably something we hadn't been doing, I'm quite sure because if it was, we would already know it. I remember he was tellin' me to do somethin', or hit this chord or somethin'. I haven't played it in a while...
Was this a typical record date?
Yeah, if it was something we knew, it was no problem, we just played & get it over with. Now and then ...
Listening to the recordings
...We're playing something, a blues...
The discography lists it as "Boogie"

... Slam got a whole solo hear... Sometimes you hear a little background beating in the back... Now this is one of Charlie's riffs... I liked Charlie, there's no getting around it, and I play a lot of his things. Lot of his songs...
Did you usually talk thing over?

What we did was as we are doing now [on the recording], we'd talk it over, and say we're gonna put this riff heard this riff there, and as we talked, we would run it down once, and then we'd play it. A talk-over.
Did a recording session allow you to talk things over more than a club date?

It was really a computerized thing in your brain, man... No, ... You just I had to remember it. Here was a guy who was blind & he remembers it, you better get on your toes... I think I insisted on this particular tune of Charlie Christians... All these riffs are talked over... Boy that man was mmh, incredibly out of this world. Play boogie woogie, do anything...
So that went over pretty good [listening to the recording] Now was back there I made a modernized riff...
So your playing was pretty modern at this point do you think?
Oh yeah. $ - - - - -
So as you said before, this was a typical recording session.

Yeah, it was just a talk thing. And then he would play a little bit of it and we had to each come in.... Funny I couldn't count no bars, I didn't know where. You'd say "Come in the 5th bar" I'd say "What."
So you would talk things over until you got it together.

Yeah, It didn't take too many times, you know. Just 2 or 3 times to find out where each riff should be or where I should come in after his solos, or how many bars that I would take -- how long I would play. And he would take it from there, and Slam would take his part. It's very interesting [the recording]. First time I've heard it, you know lately.
Do you remember doing these tunes? If I had you, Japanese Sandman, Soft Winds.

Soft winds is the only one I could remember. Like I said, I liked all of Charlie Christian's things. Because he played what I would play. He was just thinking ahead of me. I'd say 'Gee, whiz, man. That's what I was going to play.' ... But I'm probably just talking to hear myself talk. He was phenomenal man. I just had the same instinct to do that, because I never copied him riff for riff, you might say, except on certain tunes...
Did you ever have trouble with your equipment or amplifier?

No, my biggest problem was the plug being pulled out. I know I was at the Apollo Theater playing and the stage moves back and forth, you know they got it on rollers. Somehow my wire got under there and pulled the whole thing apart, oh boy. I had to play that whole performance with no nothin'. But I was there. People know. But the stagehands, they made a mistake. I don't think it was on purpose...
What other clubs did you play on 52nd street?
Yeah, I think we played another spot...
How long was the 3 Pences gig?

It was long. I have no idea how long but I know I had a tough time there. I had a pretty rough time at the 3 Pences. Came when we landed there, Ben Webster had his little 4-piece group, and he had a guitar player named Ted Walters. And he gave me a time, man. Because he was well-seasoned, and I had been playing not even two years. And he really gave me a time. Look like I made more mistakes than I ever made in my whole life, you know. Butterflies in your stomach, or whatever you want to call it. Because we were supposed to be so great. And here, I got to face another guitar player, of all things. At that particular time, hitting New York. Me with 4 strings mind you, ha ha. He was a good player. Very good player.
Was Ben Webster playing the club at the same time?
Yeah we were alternating. He had a good quartet. Denzil Best was on drums.
Tape 3 side A.
How did things work with alternating groups? Did you play on the same stage?

Oh yeah, the 3 Deuces was a small place. I don't think you could get but 80 people in there. It was very small. Maybe a hundred, I guess. Then it would be jam packed. It was a small place but it was packed every night. 'Cause they had good music. Ben Webster had a good group. I said he had 4 pieces, but he must have had 5. Yeah, he had 5, because he had to have a piano. A lot of fellas, like me, I don't need a piano. I mean, I can go without one you know. A piano is a clash there if the guy ain't together... And he's playing for himself. Like a lot of 'em make all these chords. But then guys like Ray Bryant, a lot of guys can play around you. Hank Jones, Ellis Larkins -- Those are piano players... And they know how if you're playing together, especially with a guitar, to keep out of each other's way. There's a way to do it. A lot of other guys, they don't care.
How would you compare those guys to Art Tatum?

Those guys I mentioned? Oh no, it's a different category. The guys on a frame on the wall by himself. Like Duke Ellington. How can you compare? There's no comparison. The nearest to me that could come anywhere near him is Oscar Peterson. That's my opinion, not somebody else's. I mean the nearest playing that type of thing, Bill Taylor would be next.
What time did things start at the 3 Deuces?

I think we played from 10 to four, 10 to 3:30, something like that. It was late in those days you had to play until 4 o'clock. ... I don't know if the other band started, I forget. I know we used to be playing on the bandstand and be havin' a conversation goin' on about football, baseball. Playing the music we would be talkin' about Joe DiMaggio & Yogi Berra & whatnot. And the music would be playin' goin' and we'd be talkin'. I don't know. How that could come across I don't know. But nothin' went wrong. If anything looked like it was goin' wrong, we'd just shut up. It was funny.
What was the audience like?

Quiet. You could hear a pin drop. Quiet. And I'd make this great big -- I wouldn't say error -- boner. Right in the midst of a beautiful song, boy. See playing with 4 strings is harder than a lot of people think. Because you -- I can't go no further than my D string. If I had a D flat I gotta leave that top & come jump back. And it would make me miss a lot of notes, I'd have to do too much jumpin' about -- I can't go across the board, as you might say. And it keeps me goin' up and down, up and down, so, but can't nobody else do it. That's my satisfaction. Nobody else

can do it. One fella could do fairly good at this. Took lessons from me a while. Excellent guitar player, James Charillo. I'm quite sure you know him. He could do it. I learned him all my tricks. But he's a good buddy. Very good buddy, racially
3 Deuces mixed audience?

Mixed audience, mixed audience. Musicians, nearly every musician that did anything would come in there somewhere along the line. We got more publicity by word of mouth than by the newspapers. There was no newspapers. They didn't seem to care I guess. Interested in the war and what not ... The only thing we got was the March of Times, I think they called it. Worth while, and that was so short.
Did you play jam sessions after-hours then?
Jam sessions went on uptown at a place called the Hollywood, on Seventh Avenue. It wasn't really jam sessions -- That's where Tatum would be every night.
Did you go with him?

No I never did go up there to play. I can't remember going up there to play. Because I had had a heart full of that when we got started, playing for free. And we just got through working ... Tatum would go up there, 'cause it was

his friend, his buddy. He had a piano... But I used to go by there and sit up there and have a drink. That was the only place except the place, used to be in the basement, where they used to have these hell-of-a jam session. I meant, your life was on the line. If you thought you were a piano player and you sit on the piano, there was guys lookin' over your shoulder, man. They were lookin' through you. So when you sat down, you had to play. Very few that sat down to play. And there was one saying, I don't know who said it but I think Fats Waller. He was playing somewhere and Tatum walked in & he'd say "oh, God's in the house." Now that could be backwards, I'm not sure, but I don't think it could be Tatum playing, Fats Fats walked in... that was a quote that I heard. But those guys respected one another. See Tatum could sit down and play Fats Waller style and if you shut your eyes you wouldn't know the difference. And that would keep all the piano players off him. Because he could play their style as good as they and probably better, and go on to something else. But the man never got the right PR.
How was playing at 52nd street different from other places around the country?

Well, the people didn't listen... Like I said the man never got the right public thing, you know. Pictures in the paper, or something... Why the hell didn't he get a lot of publicity. When we hit a town we just hit a town. You might see a sign "The Art Tatum" trio. But they didn't help. They can get mad with me all they want, I couldn't care less, but they didn't help. They should have pushed, just like they push other people. You know what I mean. If you know you got a good talent, you don't... No publicity. We should have had all kinds of pictures out. The pictures you see now... are so rare you can't get em...
Did you play at the Downbeat with Tatum?
Downbeat, 3 Deuces, Famous Door, Spotlight... Downbeat I don't know.
The clubs on 52nd Street were similar.
Oh yeah they were all the same, right next door to each other. We had the best who had the best drawing power, the best name that's where the people went.
Did other musicians sit in with you while you were playing there?

Yeah, I met Charlie Parker through that same sittin' in process. Very few people like it when you got your own group and you all been playing every night and you get your set routines and things. When somebody sits in that automatically makes it a jam session. But this particular night this fellow came in, I had never seen him before...
Charlie Parker? before we get into that I wanted to ask you if people sat in much with the Tatum trio.

No, there really wasn't no takers, in a way of speaking. Because they knew if they got in there, he didn't play around. I said, the only fellow that ever sat in with us that I know of was Buddy Rich. He played drums. There was no other -- I don't even remember Oscar Moore sittin' in. And he was one of the greatest guitar players around at that particular time. But he was with the King Cole trio.
Did other people play at the jams in Lovejoy's in California?
No, not that I can remember. I don't even remember one. Maybe, whoever was out there, like Ben Webster or somebody may have come in and played, but I don't remember. We did the whole thing ourselves,
And we were drawing people with the turnovers, and getting nothing but a chicken leg and a drink.
Tell me again about the breakup of the trio.

The only thing I can remember about that was we were workin' I think still at the 3 Deuces -- back again. We were in and out of there. And it was said that there would be a vacation -- we weren't gonna work for four or eight weeks or somethin'. That sounded funny 'cause we were in demand, you know. Oh yeah, it was knocke'd, it was nearly a strike. cats could play, not no gettin' around it. So it was. But they weren't into this new thing. 75% would speak against it. Say oh, man I don't know what they're playin' -- Chinese music. Bebop.
... People didn't accept it. It was hard for it to be accepted, until the musicians themselves, just like the rock and rollers - they make their parents like it if you like it or not, you're gonna have to like it sooner or later. But they made one mistake, they didn't learn the basics first...

... they was born with it...
... it was just a matter of them getting together as a unit you know what I mean - they know what each other did, but they never met, so I was a part of fate, you might say, bringin' em together, see. A little small part. Cause when Diz heard Parker, and Parker heard Diz...

... determination ...
... I couldn't go to school because... they don't teach 4 string... then I would have to try to switch to 6 string, and by the time I get anywhere, I'd be so far behind that... peers... they ready to step on my nose right now if they can. They always are. You do anything that's pretty good... like

the best gun in town, somebody gonna come lookin' for you, haha. Every time. And you think you such a great guy -- you can come in town & say I'm great -- they'd go down to the pool room and get a guy to wash you away ... I don't care what you do prize fighter, tap dancer ---

... Whoever makes that jump first -- creates somethin' just like the guy that made Frankenstein, he created somethin' nobody else could do --- If you accepted, then you got somethin' goin' . . .

I have a system here that will have you playing in a couple days, maybe even in one day if you know anything about your guitar at all, 'cause I have it laid out so its wrote in music, and then I have chord structures. And even if you can't play by music I have the notations, the dots where you put your fingers... diagrams... And the names of the notes right underneath.

... Plus I'm doing a thing I call building from the top. Most everyone -- not most, everyone starts from the root, as you might say, the root. Well I do the chord first and get that together then I put the bass in. James Charillo, he does all the editing for me and he's a very good musician and he puts the bass notes in and it comes out right, and we get students to California, Texas, correspondents you know. But they learn fast. After about -- they get a full song each lesson -- $25 or so, in town, twenty. But they get so much out of it. They learn a song. They don't learn no scales or exercise. They learn a full song, just like the music is, ... somebody else can challenge it, see if it don't come out right. So far I've had no complaints.
Is this mostly a way of building chords on the melody?

Yeah, the melody is always on top, always on top. I'll give you a little example --- [plays 'There is no greater Love'] --- I've got a hundred songs like that --- The whole thing is played in the block chord system. It's very good for vibraphone, very good. Helps --- Helps the piano player out.
When did you start writing things out like this.

I had a terrible time getting started to try to figure it out and I wasted quite a bit of time on this thing doing it another funny way I had... I... It didn't go over because I was naming chords, and the chords that I was naming were right but when you put the bass to it then it made it a different thing, you see... A lot of people start from the tonic but I come from the top.
Do you name the chords? I notice here TN A 2.
No that means top note. See that's where this thing comes, under thing you see TN 2, means top note, 2nd string... I also... Feel free to name your own chords...
Is this something you have developed recently.
Yeah, a couple years...

Take a song like Caravan, it doesn't have but one chord for quite a few bars, C. And the rest is a whole bunch of notes. But see I manage to put chords to those notes. I made every note a chord out of it. And therefore it comes out very much different.
... And every one note there's a chord...
Did you use these same kind of principals when you were playing earlier on?

No, I didn't know 'em --- Strictly single string. Everybody was single string. The only someone who turned things around was Johnny Smith. He was very good on ballads. But I notice there were quite a few notes left but that he would make into a passage... So I just tried to make my whole first chorus of the song in chords -- all chords -- no single notes period. ...
Single notes comes in blues and other songs -- tempo songs.
So you use this mostly on ballads?

Yeah, this type of thing is for ballads. Couple of times got speed, we have Cherokee and Caravan is pretty well up, its got a good bouncy tempo, and several more. Its not all ballads, but 75% ballads. ...

... Charlie Byrd, he is a great friend of mine. And he's a great guitarist, a lot of people don't know Charlie Byrd can play just about any type of jazz and latin music that there is. He's one of the few cats that can play those slow dragged-out blues. Cause we did it. We worked together several times. He can play
the blues. Best I know, he plays the blues.

... He was a master of that -- octave he could play. I don't know how he did it, but -- that's the whole good part about being anything, if you can do something someone else can't do. Or they finally tryin' to do it, and the first thing someone says, gee you sure sound like whoever the hell the person is you know. Lot of people get jealous but they should be. It's a good credit for somebody to try to play like you.
Q Do you think other people have tried to play like you?
Oh, yeah, yeah sure. I'm strictly basic. Gotta be basic. Lotta fellas skip the basics, and then when you run across one, they don't know what to do.
Q Do you think you're influenced other guitar players?

So I've heard.... Even with the blues. I've had some quotes and things, when they were naming names -- blues player. But I didn't like to be labelled no blues player.... Maybe you would like to put this in your...
'Food for Thought' -- did you write this?
Most of it, yeah...
... 'The biggest fool -- the boy who will not go to school' -- but I thought you didn't go to school much.
... I couldn't. I didn't have no family, you know.
'The best town -- where you succeed' ... 'the most agreeable companion' ... have you run into many of these among musicians?
No, man. A lotta jealousy ... A lotta fellas by me havin' the '4 string' and can play practically the same thing they can with 4 -- they don't particularly like that.
... I busted my fingers up in July...
'The cheapest, stupidest and easiest thing is finding fault' -- you must have a pretty low opinion of critics, then -- or just some critics?
Some critics. Some of 'em do you in just so. I don't know why, just to have somethin' to say. ...
"The greatest need is common sense and long green"
That's for damn sure.

Yeah, very few I didn't know, you know. I had met 'em before; we all knew each other.

No, I don't think so... No, not close up.

Oh yeah, yeah yeah I was glad to be on the scene, no gettin' around that. Just ~~on to~~ be among them. You know, I was just sittin' around lookin' at everybody [ha ha], in awe, as you might say -- to be a member of that, you know great guys like that...
Wasn't Cootie Williams there, yeah -- Cootie and I were good friends. Then I made -- records with Johnny Hodges --
In the sixties...
yeah, he even named a record after me. The little blues thing, "A tiny bit of blues," he called it...
So around that time in the mid-forties when you did the Metronome All-stars date you recorded with other well known musicians, one was with Buck Clayton. Do you have anything to say about him?
--- I used to know him. Used to come in to sit down and jam on 52nd Street when he was in town...
You made some recordings with Billie Holiday around that time also.
Yeah. Somehow, where we were playing at, she was booked in there, so. She
liked the way we played, so...
Was this on 52nd st.?
Yeah. Several clubs, I think Spotlite was one. And maybe the Famous Door, or Downbeat, one of 'em, I don't know.
So Billie liked your playing.
Yeah, I played with her quite a bit.... I had known her before in Washington, when I was playing piano, I had met her before, yeah. That was before she was Billie Holiday. She was just starting out.
What was she doing in Washington?
I think she was livin' there. Maybe she was workin' there. But she hadn't become the star yet.
Did you know her as a singer?

Yeah, I believe she was livin' in Washington, I think. I know I was livin' there and I saw her several times -- quite a few times. But --- I wasn't playin' no guitar then. And when she found that I was playing guitar she was elated, like. And she heard the little band and said, "Yeah, keep that band." You know she worked long
with us. And we worked together a long time, And lots of times.
Did you work with her in Washington?

No, not with her. Just playin' piano with this little group we had. It was funny, we got a dollar a night and a sandwich, and this was at the airport in Virginia, that's exactly what we got, and we had to get there; so, some fella used to take us there. But that's all we got. $7 a week and a sandwich a night. We could live, that's funny.
Among other accounts of your early days as a musician I saw mention of a group called the Four Dots,

That was my guitar beginning, because they would be practicin', rehearsin', you know, and they were all guitars... Let's see I may be gettin' a couple groups mixed up. The 4 Dots I think were from Washington, and we used to hang out together. But I believe it was the Harlem Highlenders that's where I met Snags Allen and I used to listen to them fellas rehearse.
Did you play with the Harlem Highlenders?

Yeah, I used to play piano off and on now and then you know. Always used to hang out together. They had a week of a group. A whole show, man. Singin', dancin, with Baby Lawrence and a couple of other dancers, and all of 'em could sing like the... Merrimacks, I believe you'd call it, at that time Tommy Dorsey had a group called the Modernaires I believe. And they could sing like that, then they could dance and play music off on top of it. It was somethin' else.
Did you wear kilts then?

Well at that time I wasn't a member. Later on, a few years later, I thought about this act. I said, 'why couldn't that act go over.' 'Cause it was a million-dollar act, they just didn't have the right manager, or agent. So I think it was 1951 -- I tried to revive it. And we went over good, you know. But still couldn't find a good manager behind us. Man it was a sight to see the bag.
Where were you playing then?

Cleveland Ohio. I went there for two weeks, stayed 2 years. And I discovered quite a few fellas, you know... Sonny Payne, I had to ask his mother, could he come out on the road, after I found out he could play. And his father was in

Chis Columbo down in Atlantic City. And they let him go out. I had to ask another fella's mother could he go out, Ray Bryant, but I heard him play, and said this cat sure could play -- young kid, you know, he couldn't go, so I had to ask his mother could he go. She ok'd it. Red Prysock had just got out of the army or navy or somethin', and... But those are some of the fellas that I helped get started in a way of speakin'. Screamin' Jay Hawkins had just got out of the airforce, I believe -- or navy or somethin'. And he kept askin' me for a job -- I didn't have no room for another fella, but he could sing the blues and he was a good, you know, good salesman.
Did you make any records with him?

No... I finally found room for him, but I never got any credit for it, he thought I was using him because I took him along. But I didn't need nobody else, you know. It was a long time before I let him do anything because I couldn't pay him. But I used to carry him along, you know, with us -- we had a couple of cars. He drove and finally I worked him in the act. And we had a six-piece act. That's when it became the Highlanders again. And I spent about

$2020 buying uniforms ad gettin' everybody fixed up. I had such a good thing goin'. I had credit with a Scottish firm here that I could call and they would send me what I wanted, didn't have to pay 'till later. We had the whole works boy, it was a sight. We opened the Apollo Theater, just like the other group and you couldn't do within' for three or 4 or 5 minutes for people laughin' at this sight. You just had to stand up there to say "cool down". It was funny. And we told jokes, danced, sang.
Q What kind of jokes did you tell?

It was strictly a Redd Foxx routine. And I had been tellin' jokes long before I heard him. Little jokes, you know. Then when I heard him I added more, and then I was really a jokester, man. But they were a little rough for those days. Go -- I had a headache with a lotta owners, man. "You can't say that type stuff up there." I say "well, hell" cha hag we got into arguments. That was the best part of my thing. We lit up Atlantic City.... And Denver, Colorado. That's where I had the trouble....

But I still didn't have couldn't make enough money. Cause we had -- 'cause we had no agent, I mean the right agent -- he would call us up, man -- I should own a piece of the Pennsylvania Turnpike -- many times
the guy would book us from here to Detroit and then from Detroit back to Washington, and then from Washington back to Chicago.
Did you do one-nighters or did you stay in places for awhile.

No, we stayed in places for a week -- two weeks, and he'd book us in Pittsburgh, book us back here, Philadelphia. Back and forth, instead of getting a routine thing so we could go one behind the other. But he had us goin' back and forth, back across that turnpike. While he's sittin' on the phone. It didn't mean a damn thing.
Did you usually have an agent --?

Yeah I had an agent, I used to do some of my own. I made enemies with 'em because I got tired of 'em. They didn't do nothin' they left me -- I'd have trouble at places I worked and I'd call them up, and one guy say "Well man you woke up my son." Now I'm way out -- where was I at -- we were in Pittsburgh I think. And I believe he was in Boston. And there was a whole lotta trouble. So it must have been about ten o'clock -- ten or eleven o'clock. And all he could find to say to me was that I woke his son up.
Now I'm in trouble up to my neck! Oh, man. Agents.
It must have been nice to stay out in Cleveland for a while. Was it a steady engagement?

Yeah, we played one place and after that engagement was up, myself and Red Prysock just hung around. We didn't have nowhere to go -- I didn't want to come back here. The old car I had just made it out there. All of us crammed in that thing, so it just did get there. So we hung around and we got this job at a place called Gleason's. Well I had to hire a piano player out there, then he knew this fella back here named Terry Potter. I think he had just came out of the army -- I'm not sure. Anyhow he was back here and he needed the gig, so Red knew him pretty good. Somehow or other I don't know if he wrote or called but anyhow he got him out there in time for this job. And the bass player, let's see I don't know where the bass player come from. Oh, from out there guy named Ike. He was married to Carmen McRae for a while. I can't think of his last name.
So you didn't bring anyone out with you to Cleveland?
Oh, when we first went there, yeah, --

I had a five-piece band. But when that engagement broke up they all left except myself and Ted Prysock. And we just hung in town, and first thing you know we got this job for a couple of weeks. That's why I say we sent for Jerry Potter. He lives right up the block from me. Very good drummer, man, excellent. And he came out and then we got a piano player and a bass out there and at that time I had made some records for Atlantic. See it helped start Atlantic Records off, in a room no larger than this -- little hotel room. Ahmet Ertegun, Herb Abrams, he had a little studio called A-1 studio. And the three of us sittin' there, and that's where Atlantic Records got started. And then they proceeded to step on everybody's nose from then on to get a step higher -- they didn't care about you after -- 'cause I made some good records there, man.
How did you get to make the records? Did they see you perform.

Yeah. Probably 52nd Street I guess, I don't know, just word-of-mouth. He came in town because Herb was with National Records and he got him because he knew -- Herb Abrams knows recording backwards. So the other fella had the money. But anyhow we got this date started
and I did the date and forgot all about it -- was called "Old Black Magic" I think was one of the records. ---

B. Atlantic records came all the way out to Cleveland to record me. Yeah they made a trip out there, while I was at this place. And I made a number called "Rock the House" and it was a hit, along with "Annie Laurie" I think was one of em -- "Frankie and Johnny" probably, and a slow blues "Blue Harlem" again -- I must have made that eight times.
When did you start playing "Frankie and Johnny" and "Annie Laurie."
There was a record company in Philadelphia called Gotham. And I made quite a few sides for them.
Were those recorded in Philadelphia?

Yeah that's when I first met Frankie Lymon. We were on the same little TV thing he made -- a little film. And I think we made it in Delaware -- Willmington Delaware. And this little kid was singin' boy -- and I was on the same thing. So in the mean time we were recording for Gotham -- we made a few sides for them. That's where "Frankie and Johnny Boogie" came. #then
Was your music any different then?
That's the time rock and roll came up.

- Yeah, we were -- call rhythm and blues, you know, and they started puttin' this hard drum things and these hard beats and they named it rock and roll, and that kind of started takin' over, and just put the jazz musician way back.
Q Did it put you way back?
But everybody way back, yeah, because see its the matter of support, you know. The kids that like rock and roll they support it. The kids, or the people that liked jazz didn't support it.

Rhythm and blues was over on a more softer volume. I think Fats Domino started off, as far as the drums is concerned, with this beat they call New Orleans beat -- or somethin' the drummer was doin' -- some kind of funny name -- somethin' like that. And the rock and rollers just enforced it more, and I stayed on -- the thing that dugged me -- this just stayed on a couple of chords -- two or three chords. And it seemed to be that the beat was the one that was carryin' everything over, not the music.
Q. Did you try to play in that kind of style at all, since it was so popular?

Yeah, but rock and roll wasn't my thing, you know. I still played rhythm and blues and boogie woogies and things. I can play a little rock, you know. Cause I have a little bit of everything musically to play.
Getting back to Billie Holiday a little bit -- you did make a couple of recordings with Billie --
Oh yeah, I made several.

All of 'em was with big bands and violins and these guys had all this music. They opened up a sheet of music man about 3 feet long. And, I didn't know nothin' about no music, but I didn't say anything, so. By the time they got through rehearsing, I had my part down, see. I just listened. Some thing happened in Germany ---- Any time any music was available that I had to be playing in big bands and things, I just listened. And then when I found out I couldn't do it I just turned the volume down, and be strummin' -- I escaped out of more traps and things.
Do you remember making a recording with Billie and Bill Taylor on bass, Joe Guy on trumpet, Bill Springer in '46 and
You did "Big Stuff"
No I don't even remember -- Billy Taylor on bass? . . .
