Yeah, I made "Good Morning Heartache," and "What is this thing called love," I think I have about 8 bars maybe on that. But otherwise you can hardly hear me on those.

"Detour Ahead," I remember that ... I can't remember too much. I remember it, but its very faint. 'Cause I remember "Detour Ahead" -- that was a tough tune. I'd like to get some of those things.

I think he musta played baritone, I think. . . .
Its funny -- these things you've made and forgot all about em. They were just gigs, you know.
Did you know Billie Holiday well?
Oh yeah I know her very good.

Well, there wasn't no jam sessions, we were just workin' together... I had some pictures I gave to some girl who was writin' a book -- I never got the pictures, a book or nothin'. One picture I had that showed...

It was a problem, not with her singin' or nothin', but with her bein' on time, you know.

Yeah.

No. Well I shouldn't say a complete abrupt 'no.' But I say no, in far as getting jobs -- you got your own jobs, you know.
Before we were talking about playing in Cleveland. Where did you go from there.

Well, we stayed there so long, I just had to get out of there -- adventure -- but I didn't have no agents. So, I got hung up, too. We went to Detroit. We stayed out there a long time. Everywhere we went we were held over. Because we had a very good entertaining act.
What were audiences like? How was playing in Cleveland and Detroit different from New York.

Ah, there was no difference. An audience is an audience except in France or a foreign country. I hate to say it but this about the U.S.A. but they surely show their appreciation ten-fold compared to people in your own country -- show their appreciation of what you're doin'. You can be playin' your heart out, and there's a guy in the next booth talkin' about the newspaper. I mean one guy -- I played at places and a guy be doin' his homework! While I'm playin' -- or readin' the newspaper and I would get mad and I would say something... 'Why the hell don't you go home and do that bleep!' -- Then I was playin' somethin' -- this is somethin' -- cause I was mad. I don't know if I should say this -- I hope they erase it, but I was at the Village Gate. I played there quite a bit, and that's a high
bandstand. Now, we're playing our hearts out. The joint is packed. And I look down and there's two guys playin' backgammon [sic]. Right underneath of me. I say, 'why you two keeps

I would push my amplifier right down in their lap. That's how mad I was, you know. How can you play backgammon, and you're in a joint I'm playin'-- Now, it didn't have to be me-- it could be anybody. They got a backgammon board down there playin'-- shufflin'-- I said-- right on the edge-- I say 'I'll push this amp right down if you don't--' and then they closed it up, and started listenin'. Ha ha. They apologized. But that's how things can catch you off, you know. 'Cause they don't know that you sit home and study and study and practice and practice, try to get the thing ready so that they can hear it. And then some guy sit up there and they talk about his grandmother, or conversation goin' on that you can hear, you know. And while you're playin'-- you can't concentrate on that cause you can hear what they're sayin'. They're talkin' loud enough, and all around, so I had to get belligerent. And I guess I got a little bad name then, but I mean they don't know what you go through tryin' to prove somethin' and show your talents, and then a guy spend big money to come hear you play and then start talkin' to his girlfriend, his wife about somethin' that happened yesterday.

And you can hear it. If they whispered it it would be bad enough, but they be talkin' loud. Conversations and arguments and you tryin' to entertain someone. And there's a guy at the next table that wants to hear it, and he gets made. So you got a confrontation, face to face thing. Its bad at times. Its disgusting. All right.

To give you an example of what I'm saying -- appreciation -- the fans -- now if the Rolling Stones -- not to even mention the Beatles -- or any group with some kind of a hit record come in town at the airport, there's 5 and 10 thousand people there to meet 'em -- supporters. Tell me just once out of your five fingers -- one time that James Brown, Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan, Flip Wilson, Redd Foxx -- the biggest of names -- King Cole -- I don't care how big the names are that's come into town to play and except for their agent and their immediate famil and -- who else -- to greet 'em -- to give 'em support, you know what I mean. They don't do that. But the rock and rollers come down and they got so many screamin' kids, even where they live at they can't live in peace.
Are things any different in other countries?
Well, no, I wouldn't say. No, I can't say that. It's a few, you know, but like the thing of it is, they don't know when you're going

gonna arrive. But see, the rock 'n' roller thing is pre-built. They know when these kids are comin' in on this plane. And who's who. And any body, just practically anybody. And there's great support to meet them at the station -- the plane to get off -- where they stay at -- the kids around. I don't give a damn who you name, Black. Not Louis Armstrong. I don't care who it was; Ray Charles, as hot as he was. The hottest black personality --
What do you think it is that way?

I don't know. I guess it's just a matter -- they supposed to do it. Whoever the personality is, that's come in -- so what else -- he's one of our great -- he's great, one of the greatest, but hell, they don't give him no support. They don't go to see him, or meet him.
Why?

Why? -- now you got a point, there -- why? It could be money, it could be transportation. But I mean out of thousands of whites, why ain't there hundreds of blacks, you know. Compared to your favorite personality that's comin' to town -- he's made a hit out on the road and he's -- oh, man -- he's comin' in town he be on this plane or this train. Even the ball players got ball players got
people to meet 'em, you know, if they win.
Q Maybe its discrimination.
No, it aint no discrimination, not among the black.
Q No I mean, the reason why black performers don't get the same kind of reception, like you were talking about. Do you think discrimination has anything to do with it?
- How do you mean, discrimination?
Q Discrimination by white people against black people.
- You can't bar nobody from goin' to the air port.
Q That's true.

- No, that's out of the question. I mean the greatest -- the only thing -- Joe Louis -- that was one of the greatest -- and Jackie Robinson -- one of the greatest of our time. They would go to see him fight or go see him play, but they never greeted him. Not once when he got off the plane or the train was there hundreds or thousands -- not hundreds or thousands, just a bunch of people to meet him -- like I said, his family or his agent would be there. And that's about the

size of it. Nobody else. So, where does your encouragement come from. When James Brown was at his hottest -- Ray Charles -- I mean even Martin Luther King, when he came to town, it was more to meet him I would say than anybody else. But it still wasn't that many -- it should have been millions, you know. A few friends -- maybe 50, 60 people -- a hundred people. Oh man, it's hard to explain. I should let -- I'll ask a question -- let them explain it themselves why didn't they support their people like the other people supported their people. Let them answer that to me -- to that. Send letters. That's the way I feel about it. Nobody, I don't care who you could name. I mean when Ella Fitzgerald was at her top. I mean who else -- especially King Cole. I mean top, top. I mean Lena Horne.
Duke Ellington.
Duke Ellington, been on a big tour of over Europe -- comin' back home -- who's there? Nobody, but their wives. Where the hell is the fans you know. So that completes that excerpt.
So getting back to your career -- you were talking about leaving Cleveland. Did you play in Philadelphia for a while?
Oh yeah, I played Philly, Philadelphia. I went to another place called the Red Foaters and I stayed up there a long time. Weeks and weeks -- come out and go back.
What made you decide to leave Cleveland?

Well I had just got the Highlanders -- this one I called the Rocking Highlanders. I tried to revive the other thing, because we were just about as near -- we didn't have the good dancers because 'cause Baby Laurence was one of the greatest dancers in the world -- was among those guys.
Did Snags Allen know that you were reviving that?

I'm quite sure -- everybody know. Yeah once it got started. So we revived it in Cleveland then we went to Detroit -- and where the hell else did we go? -- I think we went up Canada -- I'm not sure -- I'm quite sure we went to Canada, and Baltimore, and then all the theaters -- Washington, the Howard Theater.
So when did the Rockin' Highlanders break up? Or did you just stop using that name?
No, no I used the name even after we stopped wearin' the costumes. It was the Rockin' Highlanders -- we used to wear the hats, the Tam O'shanter's -- just that, and then dressed in ordinary clothes.
But we still used the name Rockin' Highlanders. We used it and used it until I had to lay off with these operations...
Tell me more about that
The operation, man, my leg was givin' me a fit.
What happened? What did it come from?
An accident, yeah.
Car accident?

Car, yeah. But it didn't develop until way late. I was like you make a bruise on your bone, but it don't happen -- after a while it just started developin' -- that's what happened -- on my hip. It really carried me through a thing for a long time with this hip. I couldn't get pain pills at that time, nothin' but aspirin and Empirins. Boy, it was a mess. And I was workin' -- the last place was a place called The Purple Manor, owned by Leon Aikens, he was a good friend of mine. In fact I'm goin' to play the prison in the midst of December -- about three weeks from now, Lake Placid -- Ray brook [?] I got a call from up there, and they want me to bring a review. Because every summer I go up Gossmer's Dock and you see [?]

the sign up there-- and carry a nice review up there every summer. Been goin' up there for quite a while. Maxine Sullivan's been up there, and Bucky Pizzarelli -- guest star, you know. So I'm gonna take a thing up to Lake Placid, or either Raybrook which is near Lake Placid, for the inmates, 'cause I got a call from there and they voted for me to come up. So I'm tryin' to take Ruth Brown and Big Nick Nicholas and my little trio, and probably a shake dancer. I'm gonna do that. It's already in the making. They'll call me next Friday and we'll set it up.
Did you ever play a prison before?
Not here -- yeah I've played prisons, sure played Baltimore and somewhere else.
What's a prison gig like?

Oh, Now you're talkin' entertainment, these guys -- well that's what they need, They need something and they really appreciate it. It's no problem. Everything is nice, you know. You can even get to hang out to a certain extent. I know quite a few fellas up there, you know. So, I'll be glad to do it. I got the personnel, it's just a matter of what the date is going be. I don't even know what the name of the prison -- I think it's Raybrook.
So, you said you played in Cleveland for a while, and then you went to Detroit and traveled around a bit -- Canada -- but you did end up in Philadelphia for quite some time too.
Oh yeah, well I was in Chicago, too, for a while, and when I hit Philadelphia --
Were you playing with a 4-piece band for the most part?
5 piece. I had a saxophone player.
You made a lot of records with those guys -- Red Prysock and Screamin' Jay.
Yeah, yeah Red Prysock.
How about Benny Golson?
Oh yeah, now this is some weird funny humor Can you imagine Benny Golson in one of these kilts? Can you imagine Tadd Dameron in one of these kilts?
Really?
That's for sure. They didn't like it. Boy, they gave me a time. 'Man I got to put this bleep on.' Ha, ha. I said 'Well, man, that's where these dollars come from -- I don't wanna put it on either
but I got it started." So they did it for a while, a short while.
Did Tadd Dameron play with you for a long time?
Yeah -- not a long time, but he played with me.
Where was that?
All around -- Philadelphia, I don't know about New York, we didn't work too much in New York except theater. But yeah he was among them.
Who were some of the other guys who played with you? This was around the late 40's -- early 50's right? The discography lists Ike Isaacs --

Ike Isaacs, that's who I couldn't think of, yeah, from Cleveland, yeah. 'Cause he was married to this girl, Carmen MacRae for a while. He advanced himself. I don't know what happened to him lately. But he was a manager and he was everything.
How did tunes like Annie Laurie go over?
Very good, very good.
Maxine Sullivan had a big hit with Loch Lomand --
did that have anything to do did that give you any idea to do that sort of thing?
No it didn't give me the idea. I just did mine to fit the costumes.

The discography lists a lot of recordings for Atlantic and Gotham at that time. Are these typical of the tunes you played in clubs: Annie Laurie, Hot Harlem, Flying Home, Park Eyes, Sidewalks of New York.
Yeah
There's a listing of a session with a singer named J.B. Summers, doing a tune called Drinkin' Beer.
- Drinkin' Beer? No. But as far as chord forming was concerned, that was is concerned, that was one of the first tunes I played, Sidewalks of New York, in all chords.
Wow, that was back in '49.

Yeah but I didn't pursue it, that was one particular tune I played and then the rest -- cause everybody was single-note, you know. Chords were all right if you were strummin' with a big band or somethin'.
So when did you get to Philadelphia-- was that in the early 50's?
Yeah, about 54, '53, '54 maybe.
Did you stay out there for a while?
Yeah, I had a house in Philly. I had a nice house in Phils, backyard.
Really? Were you married then?
No, well, separated, I'd put it. I'm still separated. But I had a nice place in Philadelphia on Market Street. And I stayed there for a while ---
That record that I made-- that's why I left Philly. It was Errol Garner promoted that.
Right, United Artists, Big Time Guitar.

Yeah, I wasn't in shape because that's when this leg of mine started to give me trouble, then I had to have an operation, I had about seven. And three pins. Some people call it a prosthesis. That was before they got to the modern thing. By the time they got to the modern thing, I was a guinea pig ---
So you weren't playing for a while.
No, I wasn't. Then they hired me.
For the record date?
Yeah. And I wasn't in shape... It wasn't good, cause I wasn't ready...
... Errol Garner...
Oh yeah, that's why he came and found me. He was givin' me a hand. I was working at the Purple Manor at the time.
Was that in Philadelphia?
No, down 125th street on the East Side, between 5th and Madison.
But you were living in Philadelphia?
No, I --- but I had just moved here, you know. Yeah I left Phils, and I came here and got a little room and got another place.
So what made you decide to come to New York?

Errol Garner was the cause of that. He gave me the date and the date was here, and I had to come back here two or three times. So I just sold out what I had in Phila --- I had a nice little place, too. Sold it out, came here.
So you weren't too active in Philadelphia as a musician.
- No
Did you know many other musicians in Philadelphia?
Sure, most everybody that came out of there, including -- oh, man what's the guy's name -- Some very, very good musicians came out of Philadelphia
Guitar player?
Tenor saxophone, mostly -- no guitars. Tenor saxophone player. Red Garland is out of Philly, he's a piano player. ... Benny Golson is from Philly, and Roy Bryant is from Philly.
Demon Spiro?

He used to hang around Minton's? ... I think he played tenor. ... Lyn Hogue was very hot property in Philadelphia. He could pack the place when no one else ... His sister played piano, and a friend of mine played guitar that I used to learn a few things. But they dressed as people from India. So that's the gimmick that took it over. They had turbans and things. ...
What was the music scene like in Philadelphia.
I think, let me see -- some good saxophone players come from there.
John Coltrane.
Coltrane. Yeah. He didn't play that type of style down in Phils.
Oh no? what did he sound like?
Regular saxophone player, you know. But he got himself a gimmick goin' and everybody followed suit.
He must have been pretty young when you heard him.
Yeah. I tell you I used to go down there, and there were a few other guys I just can't think of their names, they were very good.
The Heath Brothers?

Yeah, we played together quite a bit. Fishin' too. He's a fisherman boy. Yep, one of the best fishermen there is. When I go to Montauk, man he takes me out a lotta times. He has his boat, you know, and he catches big fish... And there's Earl Womack, a bass player -- he plays with me up til now, and a little piano player --
Now these guys couldn't read. Now how a saxophone player could learn how to play without readin' is beyond me...
What were you doing in new York after that recording session. You weren't too happy with that record.
No I wasn't too happy with it because. ch, they musta made twentz takes -- it was a mess, I just wasn't prepared for it, that's all I can say.

What was it like recording for Prestige records in the 50's and 60's?
When you made a recording for Prestige as far as I was concerned they had all the sidemen their own, and they just wanted you to front them.
But you knew Ray Bryant well.

Yeah dy that time he was also known himself. By that time -- this was a long time ago, this is from '47, '48 or somethin' like that. By this time he was established himself as an excellent pianist. He could read, gave
me a few pointers on compound triplets-- I didn't know what they were. He say "Well that's a compound triplet."
Q What is that? What is a compound triplet? A triplet with 3 quarter notes, why they call it a compound I don't know. That was the particular name at that time.

Q You made a nice record with J.C. Higginbotham-- do you remember much about that at all? Yeah well see, I procured... I got them a lot of musicians that were idle and could use a gig. Like Coleman Hawkins wasn't doin' nothin'. And I suggested him, I said "I think I could get Coleman Hawkins" 'cause he and I good friends and as soon as I asked Hawk, he said "yeah, man-- for a session, yeah." But like I said it wound up at a later date, it was his session and not mine. But he had the stronger name, naturally. But they didn't even let me-- they didn't consult me or let me know anything-- they did the same thing with Charlie Parker. Before I knew anything it was Charlie Parker's date and I was a sideman. But they wound up sendin' me the royalties, but the recognition I never got, and they didn't switch it back. That seemed kind of rude--there's a better word for it, but I mean, you know, to do that to someone that suggested them in the front

that they didn't want, and all of a sudden... they don't consult me... I had to fight for the leadership fee, through I think it was Fox -- what's that company that gets your money back for you -- Fox. Some kind of Fox, I think it's Fox. Well, they help you get your royalties, you know, back. And it was finally switched around that I could, you know. They didn't even offer me that. They could say, 'well we would like to use this guy's name, put it here cause it sells more records, but you still get your fee' you know. Which would have been all right. It was already in there cause they did it... So they did that twice that I could remember... and I was never consulted...
Some of the other records you did for Prestige included one with Jerome Richardson, Ray Bryant, Wendell Marshall and Art Taylor.

Very fine players. They elected them I'll give them credit -- they elected everybody on there. Before I know anything, they say 'we got a session for you' -- Don Schlitten did the same thing for Muse Records. They selected the people...
How about the tunes? Did you get to pick the tunes?
I got to pick most of the tunes, yeah... But they did the listening and they would release

a side that I didn't think was good as another one. Especially when you make one then take two, make three. To me one side had more to offer. But they were the selectors... That's the way it went when you got a recording session. They had the men pick -- you just play.
You mentioned a recording session earlier with Johnny Hodges in 1967 for RCA and they did a tune called 'A Tiny Bit of Blues'.

Yeah, he dedicated that to me, he named that for me. I played quite a bit on that -- We used to always hang out together, man, 'cause he drank a drink called -- what the hell was it called -- real sweet but it was strong -- Southern Comfort -- I used to drink that stuff till it ran out of my ears, and I didn't know -- which way is up --
Was it ok to drink at record sessions?

Well, it was according to whether you were offered or if you slip in, you know. But I tried my best at Erroll Garner's thing but it just didn't come out right, because at that time this leg was hurtin' so bad, I couldn't concentrate on nothin' man. And I didn't have no pills to take.

And at that time I didn't -- I don't think I had the operation. If it was it was the first one, and the first one was no good and the second one was pretty good. They gave me a spine shot, and bent me over too far and broke the cement or whatever was in that. And so this -- put a nut in there, a bolt, and that did no good -- operation. Then they finally put another whole new hip, and up to now that ain't do no good. ... [?] pound of flesh more. I'm scared to go -- they got a new thing out but I don't -- I just stand the pain, I just go along with it.
In 1968 you took a tour of Europe with Milt Buckner. How did that come about?

Oh, it was good. Milt is one of the finest guys that can take any kind of thing and laugh it off. He used to -- amaze me -- he would laugh if you dropped a pencil on the floor. He was a fun cat. I don't care what you do -- you could say, hey man, look at that bird flying by and he would break out and laugh. I mean laughin' -- no g kidelin' around -- And a musician; such a musician. I had a ball playing with Milt. What was that bass player, played with Louis Armstrong ... Arvell Shaw. He and George Wein sent us to Italy. Was at just about the last point of the boat someplace.
Was that the first time you were in Europe?

No, no -- So we go, and I think Buddy Tate was on there and Cozy Cole. We were takin' the place of Eubie Blake. So this guy asked us, 'Hey man, do me a favor, do this, I'll do this for you.' So when we come back, we stayed in Nice in France -- It's a place somethin' like Central Park. Paved's spotted all over, and you just wandered about. But it was much safer -- and it went on all day -- But there was a disagreement of me goin' somewhere with another agency over there, and there was strong words involved because just because.
How did you like playing in Europe?

Oh very good. The people accept you like I said, ten fold -- If you get a good audience here that really listens you've got -- somethin' extra special. Because the average person -- I don't care how good you are -- will have a conversation goin'. And they don't listen to the music. They hear it -- They don't give a shit. They come there, they gossip and talk over different things.
But it's not like that in Europe?
No, those people -- when you start playin' there's no noise. No noise. Till you finish.
So when you toured Europe that first time with Walt Bockner, did you stay in one place for a long time?

Well, home base was Paris. And would make our little trips and we would meet back there, and then he'd plan some more. But the home base was Paris. I used to live approximately three blocks from the Champs-Elysees. I met a few fellas over there -- Mickey Baker, he's been over there, he's really Parisian, Kenny Clarke, Memphis Slim...
What were recording sessions like in Europe?

Bad over there, very bad. They don't have the facilities, at that time. The ceiling was about 50 feet high -- a hundred feet high... but the sound just couldn't come out. They didn't have the right equipment -- then. Now, I don't know maybe now they probably have. This is ten years ago -- They didn't have any kind of equipment worthwhile.
Also in the late sixties you did a record with Illinois Jacquet. Were you happy with the way things came out on that date?

Oh yeah. I played what I was supposed to do best I could. Had a very good piano player -- Wynton Kelly. They had some things I couldn't read. I was reading a little, you know. And he got a little annoyed
because I think I was kind of holding things back, as far as the reading part goes.
Did they go over new charts on that?
I forgot what the hell it was.
They did Still King For Once in My Life, Every Day I have the blues, The blues thats me, The Gallopin' Latin...

-They named one after me. "The Blues That's me", I believe, ... But he took a tape from me that I valued very good and all I asked for was a copy of it. ... We were workin' at Buddy Rich's and the sound man had a good outfit and I paid him to make me a tape of one of the sets and the tape came out very good-- excellent. As if it was made in the studio. And I let Jacquet hear it and he said he wanted to borrow it I said yeah, you take it and copy it off and give it back. And he never did. And that's how we fell out. ... All I wanted was a copy. He was so scared that I may do something with it or somethin' I guess...
When you went to Europe with Milt Buckner the first time did you go there with other musicians? Did you play with any European musicians?
Other musicians in Europe
Yeah, we had John Letterman, trumpet and a drummer over there...
...Wallace Bishop...
...He never did progress, as you might say. Boy, he played like he was playin' in 1930. I shouldn't say that...
How did you like playing with organ players.

Well, organ groups and piano players are the cause of me playin' without one as far as today is concerned. Because I made myself adept a system that I don't need piano or organ, cause they like drove me out of my mind. With my own organ. I paid $3,000 and some dollars for an organ. My organ and I gotta find somebody to play it. And they guys -- whoever could play it they gave me a hard time. Plus I got to cart this thing around. I'd have a trailer. And -- the thing ran off, get loose a couple of times -- boy, it was a mess. And I got a 3000 dollar organ, the speaker -- now I got trouble with organ players. They give me a hard time. If they get mad they turn up all the buttons. Then you can't hear nothin' but organ. You can't hear me, period. It was so bad, I'll tell you one time I pulled the plug -- that's how bad it was. I pulled the plug out of the organ so the cat couldn't play nothin' and I went ahead and played. I keep tellin' him, man

why don't you turn that thing down a little? Then the piano players, they overload their chords. They get two hands, so they try to make two hands, and if it was possible they would put one of their feet up there to make extra notes. They got so many notes there's no room for nobody else, especially me. So, but it's beautiful guys that play man, like Hank Jones, Ray Bryant, and I mean, lot a guys that could play and keep out of each other's way and when your time comes you can do whatever you want to.
Was Milt Buckner a good organ player?
Excellent excellent. Piano and organ -- write and read.
You didn't get in each other's way, then?
No, we had no problem. Heck no. I tell you that was a fun guy. I never saw him mad. He would laugh if you dropped a screwdriver.
Did you play with European musicians over there?
Yeah, we had a couple of guys. Let's see, one was from France -- a bass player, and then they have another guy from Afghanistan. They couldn't speak no English, but they could play.
Was their playing any different from Americans?
No, I mean, swing-- they'd listen to records, you know. That's why its good to get a record that you like and listen to it and put it on tape and keep it around.
Do you do that much? You mentioned earlier that you didn't do that earlier.
No there wasn't no tapes. We had a thing out called a wire tape. I couldn't even afford that.
Do you listen to recordings now, or have you in the past.

No I listen to them in order to practice. I have a couple of types of Jimmy Rushing and its got a huge variety of songs-- a couple of albums. And I can practice with that-- put it on my amplifier and turn it up and its like a big band, you know. I even recorded some things with a big band playing and I'm-- I had it fixed up so I could play right along with 'em. And it came out good. Sound like I'm playin' with them.
You did another tour of Europe in 1970 with Jay McShann. Was it fun playing with Jay?
Oh yeah, talk about fun-- he and George

Kells, he's my buddy. He was over here the other day.... But it was just so much drinkin' goin' on, boy them guys - oh. And then everywhere we get, before we could get in town we were invited out to dinner and lunch and you didn't even have time to wash up -- clean yourself up to play your theater date, when somebody wants you to come to dinner. And they could cook -- boy, French cookin'.
Did you play a lot of theaters?
Theaters, mostly theaters. Yeah, they were concerts.
Who booked them. Was there an agent?
- Yeah, over there. Monesier, Jean Monessier. But he had a parter that was -- we didn't get along.
So you were leading the group, right?
No, well in a way of speaking, yeah, I was headlinin'. It was an all-star thing but I was headlinin' this particular one.
Did Jay McShann help get the thing together?
No no no. They got it together over there. Called whoever they want. So I had been over there before, and I did a good job with Milt. Then I was over there again with
... Panama Francis -- Arnett Cobb. And I was co-starrin' that -- between the two of us, we were both leaders.
Was that with Panama Francis?
Yeah he was there -- that's the album we made called Groovy Fours.
- Yeah.
What was it like recording there. You mentioned earlier that it wasn't as good as here in the states?

Well, the facilities they had. But in this particular place -- this was a Decca ... affiliate ... So they had a much better system. And it was small. See, the first one I made with Milt it was a great big hall, cause it could hold two or three hundred people there, that's how large it was. And they tried to record in that thing and it just didn't come out too good. But this one, -- was in a small place. Because even with the one with Milt Buckner, I think after the first try we moved to a smaller studio. Because I have pictures around here that show me in a little stall like they had fired up.
They had you in separate compartments with

headphones?
This particular-- I didn't have no headphones, but I was in a separate compartment. They weren't together with the system, there's no gettin' around that.
So, in your career in the early 1970's what are among the most memorable thing? Any concerts in particular?
We did a lot of concerts and a lot of travelin', all in Spain...
How about the Town Hall concert in 1971, that resulted in a record.

Oh, the album, yeah that was really tough on me. Yep. Well, all those heavy guys, you know, and they included me-- I'm the only black guy in there. George Benson was on there but I... his company wouldn't let him release somethin'-- anyhow he didn't get any PR at all. But he was on the program, he played last. And I was on there, and it was heavy. All those guitar players, boy. But they made an album for me. The other guys was two and three-- myself and someone else they made a whole side. And we didn't have no chance to rehearse like very little. The whole thing was done in one day. It was a long day, though-- from
about two.
... What over the last ten years or so is really outstanding about your career?
Outstanding? Let's see, well I can't say cause -- turn it off a minute
[tells of grant got from Smithsonian to make a recording. Tapes were made but recording never issued].
Did any of the record dates stand out over the last ten years?

Oh yeah, with Duke Ellington. I was at -- I think Stanley Dance was the cause of -- he threw quite a few things, he was one of the fellas that threw things my way. I may have goofed up somewhere, but he's a good friend, He writes good. But he got me with Duke Ellington on the Ed Sullivan Show and we made an album. By my shyness I didn't play. I just strummed along, because I'm waitin' for Duke to tell me to do somethin'. He never said nothin'. And the bass player, I think his name was Joe Franklin. He said, "Play man, play." Now I'm torn between -- I said well ... playin' in this man's orchestra and he ain't said nothin'. If he had said, you know, point or said play -- then. But nobody said nothin', I guess in that band everybody, just when they want to play, they go ahead and play. I don't know that. You know, I'm just there. So I was
glad to be there. I guess if he had wanted me to play, he'd have, you know.
How was it that you got there, was it through Stanley Dance?

Yeah, because I was invited to play at a place in somewhere in the Bronx they were playing, and I went up there to see him. And first thing he said, hey I thought you were gonna bring your guitar. But I don't know. How the hell do I know. I'm goin' to see him and they playin' the band is playin' he was inside but the band was playin'. And like it was a concert up there. And nobody said nothin'. I ain't the type of guy to be boastrous. What the hell did I say, What the hell I look like, little as I am goin' in that big band, and startin' something, or embarass myself or somebody say what the fuck you doin', you know. That's the way it occurred to me. When it was that they wanted me to do it, but nobody said nothin', but the bass player, and he just didn't influence me enough to go and start meddlin' around while they're doin' their thing.
What was playing the Ed Sullivan Show like?
It was all right, it was nothin'. No problems. You just went down there, rehearsed, and they had you on high platforms.
Had you ever done television before?
No -- yeah I did this thing with Frankie Lymon ... Gotham records had a lot to do with it.
How did you like recording Profound's Blue with Houston Person?

It was all right. They just -- see those. Like I say, a lot of times those fellas -- they name the tunes, they hire the musicians, they do everything. And then they hire the fella who's gonna front em. And then when things go bad, they blame it on the guy. Just like baseball, everything goes, they blame the manager -- I don't care what happens with the players -- he's the one gets fired. So, they blame it on me. And I don't even know what the hell I'm gonna do. They get it all planned -- what songs -- Profound's Blue, I said I played that enough, man. That's why they named the record that. That wasn't me. But it's blamed on me.
Over the past five years or so how has your situation been?
Well, I did a few things for George Wein. He called now and then, then he skipped a couple of years.
I saw you at Newport -- New York at SUNY at Purchase?
Yeah -- Now that was I would call that

when you think you should do somethin' for someone... A favor I guess. That was from that cement thing that was buried down there, right after that. Oh, you know the meeting that we had to put the names in the cement.
On 52nd street?

Yeah... Well I was invited down there to represent Tatum... So I accepted for him so he could get his name in the sidewalk. Now, another fella never gave me no recognition was John Hammond, I don't know why. Never recognized me -- miscellaneous I guess...
Did you ever have any dealings with him?

-- no, I tried, but -- he was there we sat next to each other -- he never said a word... So George Wein was there, and he hadn't hired me that year or the year before -- one of 'em. And when I accepted this thing he said, 'hey, I think I may have somethin' for you.' It was all right. What he gave me -- ha ha ha, I tell you. Well, I won't go into that. But he threw somethin' my way, I'll put it that way... He wasn't shit.
How did you feel about the award thing for Tatum?
It was good because it was a lot of celebrities

Oh, god. I even had pictures around here, plenty. I mean everyone was there. And for... For them to put whoever name it was in the sidewalk, and then that was that. But he threw a gig my way, for that up in Purchase, New York. Pitiful, New York, that's a better word. Man, I make myself a lot of enemies just talkin facts. The truth is, ain't no lie. Then let's see, the next time he hired me was a long time--Years.
What were some of the places you played in New York? You mentioned the Village Gate

Now here's another thing. Now for a while I was in his little group, he had a five-piece group. It was, let's see Larry Ridley, Howard, he played the piano, and myself. And we travelled. We went to -- I remember a few Universities, I think Rutgers probably was one, and we then we went to Columbus or Cincinnati Ohio or somewhere. And his little group -- I was in it. Now that tells you something. He plays good piano, you know. I give him credit. He plays damn good piano. So, and he had his little group and we'd go around for awhile, then they fell apart. I didn't do anything that's for sure. But I did turn down -- an offer because I was more insulted -- I know I shouldn't have did it -- I tell you I do things to hurt myself. Now, the whole time they were in Newport, he never called me. When it hit New York, after the first year -- then he calls me.

And I'm in a bad mood, I said, no I don't even want to work -- all this time. And it was a matter that I wanted to, and he never, you know -- and he said -- he called me back, I hung up. I said, man I don't care, I don't want the job -- all this time. Bad as I wanted to. So he called back, and he said, then he said it was an oversight. Now that don't sound right. An oversight -- me? And I said how can you play, get a guitar thing together -- one more time -- $ -- how can you do that without naming me? So he included me. But it was approximately a no-no, you know, if you don't bend too much, so I just ain't the type of cat to bend. I bend a little, but, you know.
How do you see yourself among jazz guitar players? Do you think that you influenced a few people. Some people have called you a pioneer electric guitar player.

That's possibly true because when the electric guitar first came out -- I wasn't no pioneer -- another fella I think I told you -- he had a four string but it was tuned like a banjo, and he just played pretty chords. But I just wanted to play runs --
Who was that?
A guy named, ... what the hell was his name --
It'll come to me. He wasn't that jazz -- he just made pretty chords. But I wanted to do somethin' fast. And the type of tunin' that a banjo has you can't do it -- you can't do that on that.
And you came up with these ideas around the same time as Charlie Christian did.

Yeah, and honest-to-god I had not heard of him, you know. There wasn't no records out like now. The first time I heard him he was with Benny Goodman. Well I was already playin' like that, in that type of vein, you know. I never heard him nowhere, on the radio or anything. When I first heard him he was with Benny Goodman. And come to find out I was playing along the same lines, but I wasn't copyin' him 'cause I had never heard him.
How would you say the recording industry has changed over the years as far as the jazz musician goes.

Well as far as the jazz musician goes, like I said before, they don't support 'em. If the jazz people that like jazz just supported them 25% compare to the 150% of some other people... I don't care who they are Sammy Davis -- red hot -- George Benson -- red hot He's a good friend of mine, too. He's a good friend.
When did you first meet him?

George? he used to come hear me play at a place called the Burn on 155th or 34th somewhere around there, and Lenox Avenue. And then I used to go and hear him when I first heard him around Minton's. That's when Minton's was on its last legs. And I said, damn, this cat sure can play. And I wasn't playin' at the time, I lost interest. He actually started me to go back, I said, hell I better get goin', you know. I said, I never could play that fast, but I got myself back in shape. He's the cause, he instigated. I said, listen, I said, damn, this cat plays like most of the white boys play. Fast, fast up and down thing. And very few black musicians can do that, guitarists. Very few. He, and now he's influenced a lot of guys. There's a guy named Melvin Sparks, very good we played together up near Boston. And he's one hell of a guitar player. George influenced... George has asked me things to play, you know, and I really thought he was kiddin' at first -- just to have somethin' to say, but he really meant it. This system I get if he would ever get a hold to it -- a lot of fellas, you know.
What are your thoughts about jazz music has changed over the years.
Well all I could say is guys don't look out for each other, like the other fellas do. It's

each man for himself, they don't give a damn. There's no cooperation. And they've always knockin' each other, you know, if you don't do this this good, or if I get a chance to do it I'm gonna do it my whole way, and put yourself in a cage and lock yourself from the rest of the musicians and do your thing. It's called do your thing. And cooperation is out.
What are your thoughts about the musician's union?
Union? There's nothin' I can say about them. You know, except if they catch you wrong, you're in trouble. That's all I can say.
They haven't helped you out over the years?

Oh, no they don't help you get no jobs. Now lately you could go and stand in downstairs if you want to stay there the whole day and see who they call for -- need a drummer -- we need a bass player. Then wheresever up they get the first come, first served. But now they got a new system that they, when someone calls in, senior citizen or somethin' calls in for a group, you're on line, they have a rotation thing goin'. So, I made one last week so I guess I was up that near it'll be a long time before they get round to me again cause other guys. Unless you do an excellent job. See, that makes you have to sing of songs. Like when

I first learned how to play I was called a ... request -- I played a request house. That means you play for tips more than your salary. And people throw throw songs at you your grandmother don't even know and you're got to try to remember. I had a little trick, I used to say well -- I had a very good piano player -- a guy named Sonny. Oh he was excellent. And we played at [Alabama?] and other places that was requests. They would send up money -- we would make twenty, twenty-five dollars a piece -- five piece band, six piece band in a night with tips. So we asked the guy if he comes up there with some song we don't know, we'd say him a little bit of it and he'd hum a little bit, and we got that. And we say, keep it on up, man. And then we got people right around there -- we say, you know what, you sure got a good voice, man, --- in the meantime we learn the song. ... So by the time he sing it once or twice, we got it, and we get about 20, 15, 10 dollars.
What would you say are some of the highlights of your career?
I played with three of the greatest pianists in the world. That was Art Tatum, Earl Hines, Duke Ellington. I never played with Teddy Wilson. I tried to, you know, but I mean I did that.
We didn't talk about Earl Hines much. You toured with him didn't you?
Well, I even made an album with him at some club. Very good girl singer, she was with him a long time.
What town was that in?
We started off in Canada when I joined him. It was up in Canada, let me see, I don't think it was Montreal... Toronto, I believe. I was there with him a while.
How did you like playing with Earl Hines?

Oh, good, excellent. We played at Blues Alley in Washington. We played the Blue Note in New York... We played around. Iowa--oh, that was terrible. Man, in the winter time, in December. I think we stayed up there six weeks. And it was awful, that cold up there is something else. ...

I'm the one who took that up--when I used to hear that on the radio some guy used to holler "Father Hines"--I took that up, and he loved it, he said, it bring back memories. And he played his theme song. It wasn't but three of us--four, I forgot the drummer's name. Jimmy Lewis was with us.
Over the last few years you have played the
Cooker and the West End

- Yeah I played there. We had a misunderstanding. Static, as you might say -- whatever you want to call it. I didn't knock off join in knockin' off or don't playin' the joint, or picketin' it -- whatever you want to say -- goin' on strike against it came the new owner had -- the guy wanted me to play so I played. The other guy wanted me to lay off because it was his thing, although he was in there several times when he had a blackout he was in there. He used to always be outside trying to call people across the street to the place he had. But I just stayed, so I made enemies with him [Phil Schaap]. ... He will come to me eventually and I'll be waitin' for him.

What are some of the other highlights of your career?

- - - Playing for jazzmobile. Yeah, they hire me every year just about. Jim Harrison. Well Billy Taylor is really the one that -- Jim Harrison took it from there. And Gil Anderson [Gail] Anderson ... and they hire me because I generally put a pretty good show on. I played in my own block for two years. They keep requesting it

so they give it to 'em. But I have played all over, all around 5th Avenue, 126th, 24th, but I've been playin' with Jazzmobile, that was one of the big things. And I'd have to say the festival was another.
Which festival?

George Wein's festival. And Jack Kleinsinger, yeah, very much outstanding. I have played approximately 3 or 4 concerts for him and he's a good guy to play for. I like playin' for him. And--with the N.Y.U. concerts he gives. And who else. Gossman's in the Hamptons -- cause big people come up there, -- Gossman's club in the Hamptons, they hire me just about every year just about I bring big names.
-- Did the record date with Charlie Parker stand out --

... Well, I can't say it stood out because nobody wanted him -- not 'wanted' him, that's a hell of a way to put it -- they didn't want to hire him because they didn't understand the music, but I stuck by him. So I can't say it was outstanding from that point. You know it was outstanding after it happened -- such a great guy that he was, and I was glad to be amongst personnel that new him. -- but at that particular time, no, it wasn't outstanding because it was just a gig, and
the guy didn't want him, and I said, let the manplay, what the heck. Its my gig, I can hire who I want to.
I just have one last question for you Tiny, and that is does any bods still call you Lloyd?
Well the only person that ever really called me Lloyd was Charlie Parker, all that time, he never said "Tiny" he say, "hey Lloyd." I say, "oh man, knock it off."
Aside from that any bods?
No, no one else called me Lloyd. They don't even know the name. They had a thing out on the station WBLS, you could win a hundred dollars if you could send my name in right away and nobody did.
